Author: @1Esteband
Content:
One big piece that’s missing from this story is how the Monsanto model got exported into African agriculture with USAID’s help.

USAID’s ag programs often strong‑armed many African countries into adopting exactly what Veritasium describes: proprietary “improved” seeds (hybrid and sometimes GM), plus synthetic fertilizers, plus herbicides like Roundup. In practice, access to support, credit, and technical assistance was frequently tied to taking on that whole input‑intensive package.

For small farmers who used to save and exchange local seed and rely on diversified, low‑input systems, this created a new kind of dependency. To keep the promised yields, they’re locked into a vicious cycle where they have to buy new seed and chemicals every season from a handful of companies. If they stop, the system they were pushed into collapses: yields drop, debt remains, and the traditional seed and knowledge that sustained them before has been weakened or lost. That’s not a temporary disruption – it’s a structural shift in power over seed and land.

Ecologically, this “modernization” also brings familiar second‑order effects: monocultures instead of diverse cropping, more chemical load in soil and water, and faster degradation of already fragile soils when the system is pushed on marginal land without real safeguards. In dry and semi‑dry regions, that can accelerate erosion and land degradation and contribute to local water problems. It’s not the only driver of desertification or water stress, but it’s one important part of a broader industrial agriculture pattern.

So while the video rightly exposes Monsanto’s role in the U.S. and Vietnam, an even more insidious version of the same logic was pushed by the U.S. government in parts of Africa through donor‑backed “development” projects. The result is less farmer sovereignty and more dependence on corporate inputs, with long‑term costs for communities and ecosystems that don’t show up in the glossy yield and “food security” narratives.

Author: @scottkidder9046
Content:
I think when the question is asked, “If they didn’t do anything wrong, why do they have to go through all this trouble?” really just answers itself. At the end of the video, it turns out that glyphosate is pretty safe, and yet the mere suspicion that it might not be was enough to sink the entire company and it cost them billions of dollars. Like I understand the anger and the dopamine hit we all get from feeling righteous, and I’m not even trying to defend the company, but that does answer why a company might go through so much trouble to hide results. People hear what they want to hear. I was thinking “oh my gosh, it does cause cancer doesn’t it?” And then I heard the number of people affected, and it’s basically nobody. Like just to give context, you driving your car or getting a tan is so much more likely to kill you and yet we pay money to get tans and we raise hell when there’s a 0.0001% increase in the likelihood of contracting cancer from a weed killer. I bet energy drinks are just as dangerous. Like sure, factory workers need to be protected, they need proper PPE and there needs to be protocols in place to secure their safety. They deal with these chemicals all the time and in high dosages. But the average person doesn’t need to worry about it unless they drink it or ingest it in a regular basis. 

Having the “investigative journalists” say that maybe the microbiome is disrupted and that could cause all kinds of problems… sure, that’s so specific, sounds like you figured it out. Oh wait no, you’re just guessing. Do people with compromised gut microbiomes have an increased risk of Hodgkin’s Lymphoma? Maybe. Guess what else messes with your gut microbiome, antibiotics. Guess what else? Having a bad diet. 

I get why people hate Monsanto. The way they treated farmers, their overprotectiveness of their patents, their willingness to do their own studies, to ghost write papers, the willingness of the EPA to go along with it. Agent orange is pretty much unforgivable if they knew it was causing problems. All of that is frustrating. And yet, most of the experts in a certain area are people who work at these companies. You’re never going to have someone who always works for the government and nobody else, never once taking any job within the industry they will eventually regulate. The only way you’d get that is if regulators had freedom to conduct their own experiments, sell their own products or have a salary that was comparable to what they’d make in the industry. That’s never going to happen. It could, but nobody wants to pay more taxes, including poor people.   

My hope is that people can be adults, but that’s not the pattern. The pattern is that everyone freaks out. I understand why the affected families do that. That’s obvious. But the general public loves to jump on a righteous bandwagon the second there’s an intersection between capitalistic greed and possible cancer risk increases. And then grifters easily jump on that bandwagon and make bank off of the dopamine we get by being on that bandwagon and then we stop trusting institutions, we decide that instead of fixing them we can get dopamine from feeling righteous or we can get dopamine from burning them to the ground. (even the author at the end gave some super vague statement like “well we can’t ever have a perfect system but we can put more regulations in place.” Okay which regulations?? Which ones have been tried and have been effective? Where did the system go wrong? You had a greedy business that really brought about what it was trying to avoid all by itself, and because they were greedy, they got sued and had to pay billions of dollars in damages. Where in that system did something go wrong? I mean sure things could have gone better, but do we really want the government looking over every single thing? Can we ever expect humans to be anything other than human? The world is run on greed instead of fear. It could be run on duty and social obligations, but then human networks can’t get any bigger than a few thousand people and we break into small warring tribes again. Social mobility goes away, if you’re born a slave, you die a slave, if you’re born a king, you die a king. Greed exists in all of those systems. If you’re a peasant, it doesn’t matter if you get poisoned with agent orange, you’re a peasant and the system can still bury anything it doesn’t want others to know. 

My pitch is don’t fall into the trap of being righteous and don’t fall into the trap of being apathetic. Take the world as it is. Yes, be aware, but if you’re gonna break under the weight of your awareness, then maybe just don’t bother being aware. Take the world as it is, then see if you can’t do something about it. Something was done about this company. Things have improved. We’ve gone from the company successfully hiding the danger of agent orange and getting away with it to them being sued for billions over a couple thousand people who maybe got cancer because they were exposed to a much safer product even though we really don’t know for sure. The greed isn’t gone, but the outcome is different. So yes, we can do something. I just wish people would give specific examples and if they can’t, then just leave it as “this is what happened.”

Farmer's can't plant their own seeds because the seeds aren't theirs. They signed a contract with Monsanto, to plant Monsanto's GMO seeds (and reap the benefit of increased yields and reduced costs), but agreed that they would not retain seeds from the harvest to replant. They had to purchase fresh seed from Monsanto each year .

The only farmers who have an actual point are those that did not buy seed from Monsanto but had their non GMO crops cross pollinated in the field by nearby Monsanto GMO crops. Monsanto tried to claim the resulting seeds were their intellectual property, couldn't be planted, even if the farmer didn't know about the cross polarization. The courts have told Monsanto that under these conditions, they have no claim on the seeds, crops, or farmers.

Dioxins are a group of structurally related, toxic man-made chemical compounds, primarily composed of polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins (PCDDs) and polychlorinated dibenzofurans (PCDFs), which also includes some polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs). They are persistent manufactured chemicals, meaning they never break down in the environment, soil or the animal body. These forever chemicals (including Tuflon) accumulate in animal organs, animal fats and the complete food chain.  
They are also formed as unwanted byproducts of combustion (like waste incineration) and certain higher temp. industrial processes. Exposure occurs mainly through consuming contaminated grains, and animal fats, and they are known carcinogens that can cause developmental issues, particularly in males.

Author: @xlerb2286
Content: As a kid Dad used 2,4-D on the farm every year.  It made small grain farming possible.  Wild mustard was the worst weed in those days.  It grew fast and would quickly overgrow the crops.  Farmers used to hire kids to pull mustard but it was a losing battle.  Plowing and summerfallow (leaving the land idle for a year and cultivating to control weeds) were mandatory.  And that was expensive.  Plowing is slow and summerfallow costs an entire year's crop production.   Farmers thought 2,4-D was a miracle in those days, one trip with the sprayer and every bit of mustard was gone, along with any other broadleaf weeds.  It controlled mustard so well you never even see the stuff anymore.  We never used roundup except for weed control around the buildings though.  Dad retired before roundup ready wheat was available and our growing season is too short for the then-available varieties of corn and soybeans.  But now we know Dow and Monsanto were lying from the beginning about the safety of those products.  There's not a bit of good in either company.

Author: @emjizone
Content:
In any case, any serious scientist will tell you and explain to you that *the number of studies claiming something is not a proof per se.*
A serious meta-analysis with decent chances to approach the truth in a satisfying manner, or better say in checkable and reliable manner, must take in account not only the results and the amont of results, but also the *methodologies* of each studies. *A result without a context has no scientific value. Millions of results without a context have no scientific value either.*
The knowledge isn't in the result alone. It is in *the relation between the result and how you get it.*
Any video, article, talk or piece of information you get that is telling you results without giving you any clues about *HOW* to get such results is very misleading, an *invitation to superstitions.*

How did I came to this opinion? Life experience and philosophical thinking about knowledge construction. Feel free to ask for more details and references, to ask me about *how* I get this conclusion. But please, consider to pay me if you want me to write a book about this or spend several dozens of hours exposing and explaining this to you, unless you too are broke.

You said that the DNA detach from the gold particles and integrates in cell's chromossomes. But actually ☝🤓 this DNA is a genetic engineered plasmid (a circular DNA found in bacteria) that has the sequence of the Salmonella's EPSPS enzyme in it. When they used this "genetic gun" (Technique called biobalistic) to shoot the DNA into the cells, the enzyme is expressed without integration in the chromossomes. How does these plasmids can be replicated? Every, cell has in your DNA a sequence that initiates replication. In bacteria this isn't different. The plasmid has it's own sequence that enabels it's replication and the plant cells already have the tools for replication. So whenever they start replicating, not only their chromossomes are replicated but also this foreign circular DNA. Nowadays we have the CRISPR-Cas technology that enables chromossome integration. But it didn't exist in that time. So they used classic genetic engineering (cut-and-paste).

Author: @FeanorsBest
Content:
There’s just one missing component in your whole video, which is a factual statement: 

Monsanto no longer operates as an independent company. In 2018, the German pharmaceutical and chemical giant Bayer acquired Monsanto for about $63 billion. After the merger, the Monsanto brand name was retired, and all its businesses were integrated into Bayer’s Crop Science division.

Are Monsanto’s products still on the market today?
Yes. Even though the Monsanto name has disappeared, its products (such as genetically modified seeds and the herbicide Roundup, which contains glyphosate) are still widely available, but now they are marketed under the Bayer brand.


The situation is bad in US, but I was expecting a better handling in EU, but I was wrong. In fact, The EU renewed the approval of glyphosate in 2023 for another 10 years, until December 2033.
	•	It is not banned but subject to restrictions in certain areas (e.g., parks, schools, private gardens in some countries).

	•	Around 46,500 tonnes of glyphosate active substance were sold in the EU (+3 associated countries) in 2017.
	•	This represented about 33% of all herbicide sales in the EU.
	•	Average intensity: 0.20 kg active ingredient per hectare of farmland.
	•	Higher rates in some countries (≥ 0.32 kg/ha in Denmark, Poland, the Netherlands, Portugal, France).
	•	France, Poland, Germany, Italy, and Spain are among the largest users.

Glyphosate is still widely used in UK agriculture, especially for cereals (wheat) and oilseed rape. In some years, 30–60% of fields of these crops are treated with glyphosate. Recently, the first glyphosate-resistant weed in the UK was confirmed in Kent (2025), reflecting high usage levels.
Several EU member states and local authorities have restricted non-agricultural use, while civil society groups continue to campaign for a total ban.

Author: @ChrisdeLue
Content:
I worked for a firm in New Zealand called IWD or Ivan Watkins Dow at their plant in New Plymouth. We made 245T and 24D in reactors (not Nuclear). We had to test the results from each batch, (the only machine was in the plant managers office; it was one of the first computers in New Zealand of its type) and while waiting for the results we used to read the reports that came from Altona in Australia and Freeport in America that had inhouse reporting on incidents and personnel. Those reports, to my knowledge that were never made public reported things about accidents in the plants and health issues stemming from the chemicals. 

I worked for them for about 2 years and when I left the company about 6 months later, I got a letter from the World Health Organization that asked me to fill out a questionnaire and send it back. (This was 1975 before the Internet). All of the questions related to my health and whether I had any issues from working with those chemicals. During the time I worked there I developed a Stomach Ulcer that was found when I had a Barium Meal Xray. And I remember the Doctor urging me to leave working there.
 
I did some research and found that 245T is 2,4,5-trichlorophenoxyacetic acid and 24D is 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid both of which contain Dioxin. Although both contain Dioxin which is a byproduct of the manufacturing process the 24D was not anywhere near as high in levels. 
Dioxin or 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin or TCDD which is the most harmful of the Dioxins was a contaminant in Agent Orange that was sprayed as a defoliant on Vietnam and Cambodia. TCDD is known to cause Cancer, reproductive and developmental problems. In both Vietnam and Cambodia children are still being born with deformities. And there have been documented cases of ex-service personal from both sides dying from Cancer. So, after learning all of this I could not leave fast enough. At that time, I smelled of chemicals and everything in my house smelled and did so for some years after I left. 

That was almost 50 years ago (I will be 70 in 2 months). I don't think I have any residual issues from that time, maybe I was lucky.

Content:
The history of herbicides back to chemist Franklin D. Jones, who discovered the selective weed-killing properties of the growth hormone 2,4-D. [03:03]

Monsanto produced a chemical called 2,4,5-T, but an explosion in 1949 exposed workers to a toxic byproduct called dioxin. Internal documents revealed that Monsanto knew of the danger but continued production. [05:31], [10:46]

Facing scrutiny over 2,4,5-T, Monsanto developed a new herbicide, glyphosate, marketed as "Roundup." The company then created "Roundup Ready" GMO seeds that were resistant to the herbicide, establishing a monopoly over both seeds and herbicides. [17:29], [19:45]

The video details Monsanto's aggressive business practices, including its "technology use agreement" that prevented farmers from saving or sharing seeds. The company used private investigators to sue and bankrupt farmers who violated these agreements. [23:18]

In 2015, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified glyphosate as "probably carcinogenic to humans." This led to a wave of lawsuits from cancer patients. The "Monsanto Papers" revealed that the company had ghostwritten safety studies and attempted to discredit critics. [31:31], [37:35]

German company Bayer acquired Monsanto and inherited the lawsuits, paying over $10 billion in settlements. Despite legal victories for plaintiffs, many health organizations still disagree with the IARC's classification. [40:04], [41:13]

VIDEO SUMMARY:
Seed Patents – Monsanto (and now Bayer) patented genetically modified (GM) seeds like “Roundup Ready” crops. Just like a tech company patents software, Monsanto patents the genetic traits in their seeds. By law, the company owns the rights to that genetic design.

Technology Use Agreements – When farmers buy seeds, they sign contracts that say they can only use the seeds for one planting season. Saving, replanting, or sharing seeds would violate the agreement.

Business Model – This system forces farmers to buy new seeds every year, keeping them dependent on Monsanto. It’s very profitable because farmers can’t just reuse seeds like in traditional farming.

Enforcement – Monsanto has been known to check farmers’ fields and sue those suspected of replanting patented seeds. Many farmers settled to avoid expensive legal battles.

Author: @TheEulerID
Content:
It is one of the stories of the latter part of the 20th and into the 21st century on just how much US businesses have been able to promote their own interests through funding and lobbying politicians. The every increasing scope of Intellectual Property Rights has been their greatest achievement, and has threatened the entire idea of anybody actually owning what they buy. Instead, they are being turned into licensees, who don't even have the right to repair things they buy and whose access can be turned off at the whim of a company. It doesn't matter if it's Apple, or John Deere, or media companies then it is all going the same way. You might even find yourself unable to access your own photographs.  Meanwhile, huge corporations appear to have the power to exploit personal data, the creations of others as input to train their AI systems as well as use various algorithms without much in the way of regulation. The same companies, also carry out relentless propaganda campaigns. Whilst it's not an IPR issue, the American Healthcare industry is a case in point, where huge lobbying and media power is used to protect the interests of large corporations.

It should be remembered that America came extremely close to allowing a corporation to patent about half the human genome. That is, not the patenting of a particular treatment for a genetic condition, but any use of a particular part of the genome for any purpose. Thus any company or public body wishing to make use of that part of the patented decoded genome for some purpose would have to pay a licence fee.

Author: @Hyungnam1970
Content:
There is limited evidence that human cancer risk might increase as a result of occupational exposure to large amounts of glyphosate, such as agricultural work, but no good evidence of such a risk from home use, such as in domestic gardening. The consensus among national pesticide regulatory agencies and scientific organizations is that labeled uses of glyphosate have demonstrated no evidence of human carcinogenicity. Organizations such as the Joint FAO/WHO Meeting on Pesticide Residues and the European Commission, Canadian Pest Management Regulatory Agency, and the German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment have concluded that there is no evidence that glyphosate poses a carcinogenic or genotoxic risk to humans. The final assessment of the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority in 2017 was that "glyphosate does not pose a carcinogenic risk to humans". The EPA has evaluated the carcinogenic potential of glyphosate multiple times since 1986. In 1986, glyphosate was initially classified as Group C: "Possible Human Carcinogen", but later recommended as Group D: "Not Classifiable as to Human Carcinogenicity" due to lack of statistical significance in previously examined rat tumor studies. In 1991, it was classified as Group E: "Evidence of Non-Carcinogenicity for Humans", and in 2015 and 2017, "Not Likely to be Carcinogenic to Humans".

One international scientific organization, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), classified glyphosate in Group 2A, "probably carcinogenic to humans" in 2015. The variation in classification between this agency and others has been attributed to "use of different data sets" and "methodological differences in the evaluation of the available evidence"

Author: @geoffreyM2TW
Content: Pesticides target all other organisms except the crop that is designated to be resistant. Other plants, fungi, animals, especially insects such as e.g. bees and butterflies are affected, and the small amphibians, reptiles, mammals or birds that eat the infested insects are also affected. Concern about ecosystem effects was raised by some environmentalists ever since bioengineering started in the 1970s. I am in biology and I do not think I have seen many papers on ecosystem effects of bioengineered organisms because there cannot be positions at universities funded for researchers of this kind. Professorial positions in biology are often funded by big companies or private individuals with big financial interests usually in the area of artificial intelligence, pharma and agriculture. That is the unfortunate reality. This type of research is defended by the candidate search committees as "modern science" at the expense of doing good old honest work at the lab bench with no immediate crossover applications to the industry. "Fundamental" science research has been frowned upon at least since the Margaret Thatcher years. Science used to be a gentleman's occupation. In the last few decades, however, the expenses for modern scientific projects have dramatically increased. Universitites need big money for big projects, money that will sit in their bank accounts until fully expended, so they can financially survive and compete with other universities. Someone somewhere pouring money into increasingly expensive science projects must be making a profit. There is a dark side to this trend, no matter the peer reviews and attempts to regulate the quality of research.

Content: Thank you for this video, one among the most enlightening videos you have made, in terms of how much it matters in real life. The whole thing was shameful, to anyone who like myself had been studying biology, it made it clear this was an irresponsible company that was putting science in disrepute for economic benefit. Never when I raised my hand was my question taken, the Monsanto stooges were taking questions only from people who looked outside education, maybe those who looked like farmers, old people, old ladies. It was a disgrace. Of course no word about their shady marketing tactics, the copyright on the seeds, the cross contamination or damage done to farmers not buying their products let alone lacking the scientific justification for the claim that their bioengineered pesticides inserted into the genome of plants to be released into nature were safer to humans (and the ecosystems) than those naturally evolved and present in the natural crops.

Content:
This might be interesting to know in this time of global upheaval and political tantrums and tariffs. I'm Indian, I live in India (don't worry, haven't stolen any American jobs), so this might provide some key context to the hyper dramatic hooplah around the trade 'imbalance' between India and the US and why countries like India tariff the US and other developed economies a LOT more than they tariff us. 

My father was a biotechnologist, his name is Dr. S.K.Raina. He worked for an agricultural company for the past 20 years. He was tasked to create an alternative to the Monsanto provided cotton seeds. The ones Monsanto was selling here were extremely expensive so it was out of reach for most farmers. This is in the backdrop of there being thousands of farmer suicides that were happening all across India. If farmers would have 2 or 3 failed crops, they would be under debt for the rest of their lives so many of them would commit suicide - the other alternative was to sell your farm land, and essentially become a servant/driver/rickshaw puller/laborer in some city. This used to be a life of extreme poverty and disrespect. So many of them would not choose to do that and would kill themselves. This was becoming a big issue and there was considerable government pressure on Indian companies to produce alternatives to expensive foreign imports in the agricultural sector. 

The company my father worked for was one such company that took on the task and with the help of my father, produced a local home grown GM variant of the cotton plant seed. This was 4 times cheaper than what Monsanto was selling. My father and the company he worked for went through 3 years of hell to get it approved because Monsanto first sued the company sighting IP and copyright infringement (which is what now America is doing to the Chinese). When they found no IP infringement, they began bribing local ministers who then blocked the registration of the product, sighting GM crops as destructive and damaging to the environment. This went on for 2 more years - during which Monsanto kept selling btw. 

After 2 years the government changed and the new agricultural minister of the country was an educated chap who knew exactly what was going on and basically told Monsanto to take a hike. They tried to bribe him too btw. When I asked my father how could an American company do this, it's not fair (I was much younger at the time, I wasn't familiar with the ways of Uncle Sam till then, I believed all the Hollywood hype), he chuckled and told me that in the 70's and 80's, when India was struggling with famines, American satellites would scan the country and chart weather patterns. They would know when droughts would happen much in advance and devise their foreign policy accordingly. They would charge EXORBITANT interests from loans India would take from the World Bank to feed it's people. They would also mark up grains and rice that India had to import because they knew we had no choice. 

So the next time you hear some politician talking about how tariffs from India are unfair, it is because of these reasons. India and other such countries are looking to protect themselves from the satanic greed that American and other western companies exhibit and practice.

Content:
There's a "minor" problem with "Roundup" etc.: there're several formulations, mostly glyphosate-based (but some are not).
First of all, glyphosate (alone) is believed to be "low-toxic" for humans, but what about different salts of it?
Secondly, the excipients (e.g., surfactants and preservatives) used in pesticide preparations are often toxic too (not necessarily less than the main ingredient).
That said, multi-ingredient contribution (and possibly interaction) to overall composition's toxicity needs to be researched, for every individual pesticide formulation...

Content: For nearly 23 years I used a shot of roundup as an additive in my morning cereal. At first, like you would suppose, it loosened my bowels as it tore through the natural flora of my gut. In my bacchanalian state, I actually relieved myself in my wife’s favorite potted plant.  It presented “fall colors” by sun-up and was dead by noon. The next morning she had tossed out all my chilled roundup, thus concluding an era. These days I use a hoe and a weed eater and no longer make jokes about “watering” the weeds.

Content:
Thalidomide, (Contergan and Thalomid)
Thalidomide, developed by the West German pharmaceutical company marketed internationally to pregnant women in the late 1950's and early 1960's as a treatment for morning sickness but was soon used for treating a wide range of other conditions, including colds, flu, nausea. 
It was sold under the name Contergan in Germany, and elsewhere as Distaval.
The drug harmed around 5,000 people in Germany alone, of whom around 2,400 are still alive.
Many victims were born with missing arms or legs, malformed limbs or severe nerve damage.
In November 1961, thalidomide was taken off the market due to massive pressure from the press and public.
No-one knows how many miscarriages the drug caused, but it's estimated that, in Germany alone, Thalidomide led to the death of approximately 2,000 children and serious birth defects in more than 10,000 children, about 5,000 of them in West Germany.
It is widely believed that as many as 100,000 babies were affected by the drug in total.
Many were too damaged to survive for long.
Some were still born or died very soon after birth.

Now, 50 years later, the National Institute for Clinical Excellence has recommended thalidomide for multiple myeloma, a cancer of the bone marrow.
Now, decades later, thalidomide is being used to treat a skin condition and cancer.
Thalidomide, the cause of the biggest medical scandal of the last century, is today recommended for use across the NHS.
The decision marks a watershed in the drug's slow return to respectability.
For years it was shunned, but in the 1990s it was shown to be effective in the treatment of leprosy.
Further research suggested the mechanism by which it caused birth deformities, through limiting the blood supply to the foetus's limbs, might be harnessed as a treatment for cancer, by inhibiting the growth of blood vessels that feed tumours.

In Britain, thalidomide has been used to treat brain cancer, kidney cancer and Kaposi's sarcoma, a cancer involving the blood vessels of the skin.
Thalidomide is prescribed in Brazil, where there are a large number of leprosy patients, but children are still being born today in South America with limb defects because of ignorance of its effects in pregnancy.

Author: @The_KnowBuddy
Content:
Fun fact: virtually EVERY wheat field on the planet gets sprayed with glyphosate by default, not because of weeds or pests but because it is standard practice in a process called desiccation where wheat stalks are made to wither and die lest they sprout flowers before harvesting (e.g. following untimely rainfall, in which case the entire field would become useless - sprouted seeds means no wheat). That, in turn, means that every loaf of bread you buy from the supermarket will by default contain traces of glyphosate, unless marked 'organic', which is very expensive. Which is why I buy my own organic flour, add distilled water, Himalayan sea salt, organic coconut sugar and organic extra virgin olive oil (from a glass bottle) and bake my own bread every day. 5 minutes to prepare and the bread-maker makes it in less than 2 hours. Fresh, warm, soft, home-made organic bread on the table every day. Smells and tastes nice!

One of the many things I do to stay healthy after a lifetime of research. Most of the things I do you've never even heard of. Not even from Bryan Johnson. All simple things. I could write a volume, but who has time And who would read it anyway? Well, I hope this one thing will help someone out there, since this video was about glyphosate. May you all have a long, healthy and happy life.

Content: I would also like to point out that California’s water rights system creates another layer of control over farmers and gardeners. Large agricultural operations benefit from subsidized water through projects like the Central Valley Project and the State Water Project, with some farms receiving the majority of available irrigation. This allocation has environmental impacts, such as groundwater depletion, and raises equity concerns, showing that, much like seed patents, access to vital resources is heavily skewed toward powerful corporate and agricultural interests.

Author: @bernardhirschel6503
Content: I was looking forward to learning about the evidence there is (of roundup's carcinogenicity or lack thereof).  But this was disappointing.  A collection of anecdotes, like mice with kidney lesions in one study, or farmers with NHL, is not evidence.  You would need comparisons, like for instance of farmers exposed to Roundup vs farmers not exposed, with sample sizes, confidence intervals etc.  None of this was in the video.  Likewise, while the efforts of Monsanto to influence the "scientific" publications were justly criticized, there was zero mention of bias going in the other direction, like the allure of a 289 million dollar settlement for further lawsuits.  No mention of the possible hazard of roundup alternatives and substitutes, lot of "maybes", "could"  in mentioning possible risks of Roundup, and misuse of that common trope of media discussions of risk:  "cannot be excluded".  Strictly speaking, the absence of risk cannot be proved for anything - THAT could be the topic of another of your videos.  Not sexy maybe, but a service to the public's understanding of science.

Author: @daymien-b3e
Content:
For thousands of years, farming worked on a simple cycle: plant seeds, harvest crops, and save part of the harvest to replant next season. But in modern industrial agriculture, this ancient practice has been largely outlawed—not because seeds suddenly stopped working, but because of patent law and corporate control over seed genetics.

1. The Rise of Patented Seeds

Companies like Monsanto (now owned by Bayer) pioneered genetically modified (GMO) crops that are resistant to herbicides or pests.

These seeds are legally protected under intellectual property law, meaning the company owns the “design” of the seed.

When a farmer buys these seeds, they sign a contract agreeing not to save and replant them.

2. "Seed Licensing," Not Seed Ownership

Farmers don’t actually “own” the seeds they buy—they’re licensing them for one-time use.

If they save seeds and replant without permission, they risk lawsuits for patent infringement.

There have been high-profile cases where farmers who unintentionally ended up with patented seeds in their fields were still sued.

3. Hybrid Varieties and "Terminator Seeds"

Even outside of GMOs, many hybrid seeds don’t reliably produce the same quality crop when replanted—forcing farmers back to the market each season.

Though “terminator seed” technology (making seeds sterile after one use) was never commercialized due to backlash, the idea underscores how control is built into the system.

4. The Impact on Farmers

Farmers become dependent on corporations for seeds every season.

Costs rise, and traditional seed-saving practices vanish.

This has ripple effects on biodiversity, as local and heirloom seed varieties are abandoned in favor of patented strains.

5. Why This Matters to Everyone

Food security becomes tied to a handful of multinational corporations.

Legal battles discourage farmers from resisting, even if saving seeds is more natural and sustainable.

It raises deep ethical questions: Should life be patentable? Should farmers lose a right as old as agriculture itself?

Glyphosate has the potential to be safe if we use it safely and make sure we aren’t contaminating the food supply with it.

Author: @sweeney5296
Content: The crucial questions that need to be answered here are: 1. What dose in mg/kg is on average internalized by humans during glyphosate application, both respiratory and transdermal routes, which would vary based on ambient temperature, product concentration, wind, PPE usage, etc. (would require serum quantification), 2) how does the baseline incidence of non-hodgkin lymphoma in non-exposed people compare to those who are  occupationally exposed to glyphosate, and is the incidence statistically different given that NHL is not uncommon (would require a large meta-analysis), 3) has any molecular mechanism of carcinogenesis been proposed or documented, and if so, what is it? 4) the repurcussions on food supply/farming if the product is outlawed could be devastating.  The only difference between many therapeutic pharmacological agents accomplishing a desired outcome versus toxicity is frequently simply the dose an organism absorbs. Given that glyphosate works well for its intended purpose, is not impressively volatile in air or hard to sequester with PPE, does not persist long in soil, has poor transdermal absorption, etc suggests that if you're exercising reasonable caution during application, blaming it as causative for lymphoma is akin to blaming the increased use of smartphones for the rising incidence of colon cancer.  Could be, but correlation isn't causation without stronger evidence. No question, Monsanto is obviously focused on their financial gains and is trying to obfuscate and act like the product is harmless, which I'm sure it isn't.  The point is that almost everything we use and rely upon is harmful when used inappropriately or excessively, and precautions need to be followed.  Shame on the manufacturer for pretending it's harmless and not warning consumers about the potential for carcinogenicity, but glyphosate is still a useful tool, and can be used reasonably safely.  Look at gasoline, ethanol, motor oil, BBQ grilling, sunshine, merely existing on earth being constantly bombarded by gamma rays from natural background radiation, radon, etc. All known carcinogens.  We just try to mitigate exposure.  I'm a physician and a scientist, and I have no dog in this fight other than seeking pharmacological evidence.  Farmers don't drink glyphosate or inject it like the poor rats we use to test it, so without measuring serum levels after comon exposure through routine agricultural application, we're comparing apples to oranges.

Author: @abhishekkumarsuman422
Content:
India does not allow patents on seeds, plants, or animals under the Indian Patent Act, 1970. Instead, it has the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001 (PPV&FR).

Farmers’ rights under PPV&FR:

Farmers can save, reuse, exchange, and even sell farm-saved seeds (except branded seeds).

This is explicitly protected, making it very different from the U.S. model.

Legal disputes:

Monsanto got into multiple fights with Indian authorities and seed companies over royalty fees.

In 2016, the government cut trait fees (royalties), which Monsanto challenged in court. Eventually, Monsanto lost some ground as India asserted farmer-centric policies.




---

🔑 The Difference

In the U.S., Monsanto could legally enforce patents and stop seed saving.

In India, the law protects farmers’ rights, so Monsanto’s control is indirect (through hybrids and licensing agreements), not absolute.


That’s why Monsanto is powerful in certain niches in India (glyphosate, Bt cotton hybrids, maize hybrids), but it never achieved the same monopoly-like grip that it managed in the U.S. seed market.

Content: We actually sued Monsanto before for biological attack. I was part of an indigenous crop preservation effort on a subsidized farm in upstate New York. Surrounding major Monsanto run farms cross bred with our corn. Cross breeding white/indian corn with yellow sweet corns ruins the crop, literally poisoning and killing the corn. Monsanto then tried to go after US for infecting our corn. They gave us this patent infringement crap. But because we were a nonprofit organization full of NATIVE AMERICANS growing indigenous corns from century old seeds they couldn’t prove we profited off them. They kept ruining our corn. So we counter sued for destruction of property. They now have what’s essentially a corn restraining order. Their corn fields are limited to a set amount of feet from our property line. It really let us grow successful crops. Unfortunately life finds a way because a good 1/5th of our corn still cross breeds with their corn.

Content: As a farmer I want to weigh in on this a bit. At least in crop farming (wheat, beans, and corn) glyphosate applications occur at least 2 months typically before harvest. This cannot be applied less than a week before harvest and most people wait until around 2 weeks so the wheat can dry down to around 13.5% moisture. 22oz an acre is typical application rate. Im telling you all this to let you know that the exposure rate is near zero by the time it is harvested.

Author: @aerosyne
Content:
Solid video, although the wind-up to get to the title in the topic was longer than I anticipated, especially because the whole debacle of Monsanto's own patented seeds is rife with misinformation and wasn't really touched on enough in a video supposedly about that problem.

Yes, you cannot plant a Monsanto seed, grow it to fruit, and then save those seeds legally. I'm sure there are farmers who do this by the thousands by buying up smaller & smaller volumes year on year and supplanting with their saved seeds, or those who call for trial/sample packs to test them, and then never go full bore utilizing Monsanto. There are certainly farmers who are less scrupulous who know of this happening, and take those competitors out at the behest of Monsanto, or for other reasons. The issue is, as stated, because of how Monsanto came to the chemical formula for their GMO plants that can handle their line of agricides, and that by saving those seeds, you're stealing the benefit of said chemical formula.

The problem is that the only way Monsanto could ever prove that you broke the agreement is if, at no point, did your crop cross-pollinate with another crop. By providing you with enough corn seeds, as an example, they could achieve such an end because if you're the only guy for ten acres growing corn and using Monsanto seeds, what else is there to cross-pollinate with? The same applies if you were to take an ear at season's end, synthesize the chemical formula in your own lab, and then just manufacture it and never buy from Monsanto again; these are both cut & dry theft. However, what if you have a field of flint corn, a field of dent corn, a field of sweet corn, a field of popcorn, and a field of old world maize? For those that don't know, the corn you eat isn't the same corn that goes into cornmeal or animal feed, or becomes poppable; the same applies to all other vegetables. This is why, if you grow a cherry tomato and a beefsteak tomato next to each other, you have a great chance of coming up with some weird hybrids on either vine in addition to what you expect; this is the result of natural cross-pollination, and mixing flint corn and sweet corn can result in something gross, or possibly something in the middle that can be ground or cooked with acceptable results either way.

This is important because for Monsanto to win their cases that people bring up about farmers getting sued for the seed saving, there has to be deliberacy. The obvious reason why nobody is posting links in the comment is because any time farmers have been caught & sued is because they copied the formula one-for-one. Any time there's been natural hybridization, Monsanto has lost, because the company is required to prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that the resulting plant that might now have some amount of the Round-up resistance was intentional. Thus, unless you know exactly what in the heck you're doing or have a genetic lab somewhere on your farm or home, chances are good no Monsanto goon is going to come and fire-squad you.

Also, if you want farms to be less reliant on Monsanto, start growing your own food. The home customer has far more variability & choice, and not only will then commercial farms have to produce as much, but you having nearby plants will naturally hybridize their crops, kneecapping Monsanto and others. Double also, it goes without saying, but don't drink chemicals, especially when they're concentrated. Even if 2,4-D was fine in aerosolized amounts, consistent contact with large volumes would've eventually produced toxicity at some point short of the Dioxin problem.

Author: @JosephLMcCord
Content:
I don't have the time at the moment to listen to this all the way through - please forgive me for that - but I just want to state the facts as I understand them at least, anyway.

While it may be true that seed companies price-gouge farmers - in a sense there wouldn't be any point in re-planted seeds harvested from plants grown from them, anyway.  The reason for that and the reason that farmers don't have many alternatives is because of the nature of "hybrid vigor" in grass plants, such as wheats.  This is a biologically-evolved trait specific to those kinds of plants whose function must be to increase the chances of accidentally created hybrid strains in natural environments to propagate their uniqueness during the first generation or two - after hybridization.  The _immediate_ generation of plants created by hybridization of strains produces a greater number of seeds than either of the parent strains of plants would have done.  This is of great importance to present-day agriculture because of its need to increase yields, as much as possible.  But the increased yield of seeds will disappear within the newly hybridized plants within a few generations of replanting.  It starts to fade, already, even with the second generation.  So for as long as there's a need to maximize yields in this - there is really no choice but for farmers to a first-generation newly-hybridized strain of plants.  Whether they have a legal right to do otherwise or not, really doesn't matter.  The enhanced seed yield trait would disappear altogether within a few generations of re-planting - and it would already be beginning to fade with the first generation of re-planting.

Content: As a scientist I have a problem with the analysis done in this video. Yes it is important to concider conflicts of interest and that is why it is very important to cite them in your papers. But it is really not surprising to me that the main researcher on a specific product work for the company making said produtct ! So for me the most important thing about all this research is not who made it but what were the tests, the experiments done, the sample size ? What are the raw results of thoses experiments? Were they replicated by others labs? Scientific papers are not opinion piece by famous researchers. They are desscriptions of real life analysis that any other lab can try themselfs. Of course you can always lie and forge your results but anyone replicating your study would see that they dont have the same results and publish that themselves. I dont care that the guy was funded by monsanto or not. If they were able to show that on average farmers using roundup have exactly the same amount of cancer as others famers and if others labs get the sames results then I believe it. Author: @jon_j__
Content:
The title of this video is about "not replanting", but that's only a few minutes of the total runtime. The non-replantability thing is a great distraction from the true issue here - the toxicity of these herbicides. I say it's a distraction because the truth about replantability is nuanced (see below) - and because *the carcinogen/toxic issue is so much worse*. The video's title is really focusing on the wrong issue.

A bit more of the nuance around replantability:


(1) While Monsanto did indeed use heavy-handed scare tactics to try to protect their GMO crops, they backed off pretty quickly. Going around scaring people into line with baseless legal threats is corporate bullying, and it's not right, but it's also very common.

(2) For farmers in developed countries, the choice is: GMO, hybrid (eg. "organic"), or go out of business. The thing about hybrid crops is that you *also* can't save part of your harvest for replanting, but this time for technical reasons - the harvested crops are either sterile or have very unfavourable genetics. So, yes, it's *legally* impossible to replant Monsanto's GMO crops, but it's *technically* impossible to replant their main competition. So, in the one narrow sense of replantability, there is no important difference.

(3) The focus on lack of replantability stokes unjustified fears of GMO crops, which have so much potential to do good for the world, and it makes it even harder to properly test them for the justified fears (eg. long-term toxicity).

Author: @MarcosCapixaba
Content:
### **Summary: The History and Controversy of Monsanto**

#### **I. Introduction: A Modern Conflict**
*   **Inciting Incident:** In 2016, Arkansas farmer Mike Wallace was murdered, not over money or land, but over a herbicide.
*   **The Central Subject:** The video investigates Monsanto, a global agricultural giant, alleging its practices created fear, pitted farmers against each other, and established a near-monopoly.
*   **Basis of Investigation:** The narrative is built on publicly available documents, recordings, and third-party opinions.

#### **II. The Origin of Selective Herbicides (1940s)**
*   **Inventor:** Chemist Franklin D. Jones sought to kill poison ivy that afflicted his children.
*   **Discovery:** He found that the synthetic growth hormone **2,4-D**, when applied heavily, caused plants to undergo unsustainable growth and die—effectively "plant cancer in a bottle."
*   **Key Feature:** 2,4-D was **selective**; it killed broad-leaved weeds (dandelions, ivy) but spared grass crops (wheat, corn, barley).
*   **Improvement:** Adding a third chlorine created **2,4,5-T**, which was even more selective.
*   **Impact:** These were the first viable selective herbicides, revolutionizing weed control in agriculture and landscaping. Jones patented them in 1945.

#### **III. Monsanto's Entry and the Dioxin Problem**
*   **Monsanto's Role:** The chemical company began mass-producing 2,4,5-T.
*   **The 1949 Explosion:** An explosion at Monsanto's Nitro, West Virginia factory covered workers in a chemical powder, causing severe skin lesions and illnesses. The cause was unknown.
*   **The Discovery of Dioxin (1957):** German dermatologist Karl Schulz identified the culprit: **dioxin**, a highly toxic byproduct formed in trace amounts during the 2,4,5-T manufacturing process if temperatures spiked.
*   **Corporate Knowledge:** German companies warned Monsanto and Dow about dioxin contamination. Both U.S. companies claimed they never received or misfiled the warnings.

#### **IV. Agent Orange and the Vietnam War (1960s)**
*   **Use in War:** The U.S. military used **Agent Orange** (a 50/50 mix of 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T) to destroy jungles in Vietnam during the war.
*   **Internal Knowledge:** Internal letters show Monsanto and Dow knew dioxin was "the most toxic compound" they had experienced, causing severe health issues.
*   **Consequences:** Despite this knowledge, no warnings were issued to the government. Millions of liters were sprayed, leading to an estimated 3 million people suffering from cancer, skin diseases, and birth defects.
*   **Backlash:** Public outrage and regulatory scrutiny over dioxin threatened to phase out 2,4,5-T, endangering Monsanto's business.

#### **V. The "Miracle" of Roundup and Glyphosate**
*   **The Discovery (1970):** Monsanto chemist John E. Franz discovered **glyphosate**, an extremely potent herbicide.
*   **Mechanism:** Glyphosate blocks the **EPSPS enzyme**, crippling the **Shikimate pathway** (essential for plants to create amino acids). This pathway does not exist in humans or animals.
*   **Marketing:** Marketed as **Roundup**, it was proclaimed biodegradable, safer than table salt, and effective against all weeds.
*   **Business Model:** It enabled "no-till farming" and became a billion-dollar product. Its molecular uniqueness meant competitors could not easily create similar herbicides before its patent expired in 2000.

#### **VI. Creating a Monopoly: Roundup Ready Seeds**
*   **The Problem:** Roundup killed everything, including crops, limiting its use.
*   **The Solution:** Monsanto genetically engineered crops to be resistant to Roundup by inserting a modified bacterial gene that produced a glyphosate-resistant EPSPS enzyme.
*   **The System:** They created **Roundup Ready seeds** for soy, corn, and cotton, sold as a package with Roundup herbicide.
*   **The Contract:** Farmers had to sign a **Technology Use Agreement** that:
    *   Prohibited saving seeds from one harvest to plant the next.
    *   Prohibited sharing or selling seeds.
    *   Allowed Monsanto agents to inspect their fields.

#### **VII. Enforcement and Cultural Impact ("The Crop Mafia")**
*   **Aggressive Tactics:** Monsanto employed a culture of fear to enforce its patents:
    *   A toll-free snitch line (1-800-ROUNDUP) for reporting neighbors.
    *   Investigations by private detectives and ex-cops.
    *   Aerial surveillance of farms.
    *   Lawsuits against farmers for patent infringement, resulting in over 400 lawsuits and $20 million in collected damages.
*   **Social Division:** This created mistrust and turned neighbors against each other, culminating in conflicts like the murder of Mike Wallace, which was linked to herbicide drift disputes.

#### **VIII. The Fall: The Monsanto Papers and Lawsuits**
*   **The Catalyst (2015):** The **International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC)** classified glyphosate as a "**probable carcinogen**," specifically linking it to non-Hodgkin's lymphoma (NHL). This contradicted the EPA and WHO.
*   **The Investigation:** Lawyer Brent Wisner, representing cancer victims, forced Monsanto to release internal documents—**"The Monsanto Papers."**
*   **Revealed Misconduct:** The documents showed:
    *   **Ghostwriting Studies:** Monsanto secretly wrote key safety studies (e.g., the Williams et al. paper) and paid academics to put their names on them.
    *   **Influencing Regulators:** Colluding with EPA officials to suppress concerns and kill critical research.
    *   **The "Let Nothing Go" Strategy:** Deploying a PR army to discredit critics and dominate online discourse.
*   **The Aftermath:** The evidence led to over 11,000 lawsuits from plaintiffs with NHL. Monsanto was acquired by **Bayer** in 2018, which inherited the liability. Bayer has since settled over 100,000 cases for more than $10 billion.

#### **IX. Conclusion: How Dangerous is Roundup?**
*   **The Risk:** IARC's concern centers on **genotoxicity** (DNA damage from high exposure, e.g., in farmers) and potential disruption of the gut **microbiome**.
*   **Context:** Glyphosate is a "probable carcinogen" (IARC Group 2A), a category that also includes red meat and night-shift work. It is considered less potent than "known carcinogens" like tobacco or alcohol.
*   **The Real Issue:** The video argues the greater scandal is not necessarily the toxicity of glyphosate itself, but **Monsanto's systematic manipulation of science, regulators, and public opinion** to protect its product and monopoly.
*   **Present Day:** Due to public backlash and widespread weed resistance, Bayer has removed glyphosate from consumer Roundup products, replacing it with its original herbicide, **2,4-D**.

Content:
11:27 It's pretty misleading to depict Agent Orange as an outcome of "the president of South Vietnam" having a little whoopsy-daisy while fighting "the newly founded Viet Cong" and accidentally poisoning his own people while trying to save them. 

The historical context is that Vietnam had been a French colony before being occupied by the Japanese during WWII, with a local resistance movement consisting primarily of communists. As WWII was ending, the communist-led resistance declared Vietnam to be an independent country, expecting Western support, but instead the U.S. provided geopolitical backing for a futile French effort to reoccupy its former colony. The partition was supposed to be a temporary arrangement after the communists won a decisive victory over the French in the northern half of the country, with jointly-supervised elections to determine the future of Vietnam as a united country. Instead, the U.S. and the local southern administration (a military dictatorship) were genuinely worried that the communists would end up winning the elections, so they cancelled the plan and acted as if a permanent partition had been the goal all along, depicting the situation as if the humble little country of "South Vietnam" had suddenly come under attack by foreign communist invaders from the totally-separate country of "North Vietnam".


In short, the local Vietnamese populations in the defoliated southern jungle regions tended to be broadly supportive toward the communist insurgents (who had been resisting a tag-team of outside colonial occupiers for decades) and suspicious toward the government in Saigon (who they viewed as quislings for the latest colonial occupier) so the government in turn was probably perfectly content to see those people and their homes poisoned.

Author: @shadowfaxcrx5141
Content:
What gets glossed over here is that the farmers choose to sign the Monsanto contract. They could (and still can) go with non-GMO seeds that don't come with contractual obligations, but they choose not to because they make more money if they sign the contract.

Monsanto has turned seed economics into something of a software model: You buy a license to plant the seed one time, but you're not allowed to make copies of it. Is that an ideal model for farmers? No, but it's one that is fully disclosed every time the farmer signs the seed contract. If you don't like the contract, don't sign it and use someone else's seeds.

That's not to say Monsanto isn't evil, but on that one point, the farmers went into this with eyes open because they wanted greater crop yields, and now want to unilaterally sweeten the deal they agreed to.

Author: @Jason-7212
Content: This just one of the problems that Monsanto caused.  They were a company that were known for their environmental contamination, poor worker safety practices, and poor plant maintenance.  They had multiple fires and explosions at their various plant sites around the world that killed and injured many of their workers and the people living around their plants.  To this day several former Monsanto chemical plant sites are still chemically contaminated and there are several environmental Superfund sites that are associated with Monsanto here in the US.  Speaking on the topic of Agent Orange.  That chemical was still being produced in the 1990''s under the name 'Paraquat'.  In Texas it could only be obtained and used by companies and individuals with a state applicators license.  Paraquat, unlike 'Roundup', works almost instantly on vegetation with visible signs of plant death within minutes or 1 - 2 hours at most, whereas Roundup usually took 8 - 24 hours for signs of plant death.  In 1988 I worked for RiceTec, which was a division of Farms of Texas, seed rice producer and research company that was also affiliated with Texas A&M University.  We used Paraguat  in our research greenhouses and around the research plots.  Our normal method of application was to mix the syrupy brown chemical with water and then soak short lengths of hemp rope in this.  We would rub the damp rope by hand on the specific plants we intended to kill.  A one-foot length of damp rope rubbed on the plants just above the ground on the plants to kill would wipe out these selected plants without harming those we wished to keep.  The only safety precautions needed were chemical gloves and eye protection.

Author: @cesarrios5778
Content:
I remember trying to discuss this in a paper for law school, at that time i'd read a book about Marie Monique Robin "Le Monde Selon Monsanto" / "The world according Monsanto", I got outraged, and tried raising concerns about the issue, but almost no one really cared. 
Here in Brazil, we have a foundational legal principle called the Precautionary Principle. It encompasses the environment in broad terms, stating that any project with a potential environmental impact must be exhaustively studied to prevent all irreversible damage to nature.

I would argue that Monsanto is responsible for five main issues:

Potential consumer health issues (I say "potential" because every attempt to study them has been shut down).

Soil contamination from extremely aggressive chemicals. Leading to neighboring cutures to sign into monsanto.

A production monopoly created through the tie-in sale of GMO seeds and pesticides.

The forced displacement of the few remaining medium and family-owned farms in Brazil.

The acceleration of deforestation caused by rapid soil erosion and degradation from intense production. This degradation leads to a cycle where more forest must be cleared to maintain productive land area.

This is especially critical in Brazil, a country where 29% of our GDP comes from agribusiness—a sector that also represents 45 to 52% of our exports. We are a nation responsible for a significant portion of the world's food production, yet many of our own people still starve. Meanwhile, farmland owners pocket around $110 billion per year through various government incentives, funneling these investments into offshore accounts.


I acknowledge that legislation is, although far from perfect, in places like the USA or EU, much better than Brazil, but it serves nothing if the food people eat is produced through even more agressive pesticides abroad and consumed in your respective countries, you end up consuming a product full of poison, though not produced nationally. 


I admire your determination. Keep spreading awareness about this.

Author: @44beebe
Content: I grew up on a farm.  This was good until 26:10 .  It's not true at all that roundup ready crops were adopted out of fear that the neighbors spraying their crops would kill your crops.  That would be illegal and the neighbor would be liable for the damage.  Roundup ready was simply a really easy way to effectively control weeds that was worth the cost for growers to adopt it.  Don't try to convince people that they were "forced" into using roundup ready because that simply isn't true and is a ridiculous statement in the eyes of farmers.  Nobody was forced or compelled by outside forces, it was just a new technology that most farmers were eager to adopt.  It's like saying that early farmers were forced to start using tractors instead of horses to plow their land.  The only reason one might feel forced is because it was such an easy way to improve yields and they wouldn't be able to compete with the neighbors if they didn't adopt the technology.  I only know this because I and many of my friends are farmers who experienced the rise of roundup ready crops.  Being able to control weeds is extremely effective at improving yields, that's why it's worth the cost for most growers.  I am not pro-monsanto, I will always buy the generic brands of glyphosate, but this kind of fear mongering and insertion of false information in order to drive a reaction just makes me doubt everything in the video.  Same thing goes when you talk about the guy getting non-hodgkins lymphoma.  That's simply one anecdote and isn't really backed up by the data or the facts.  The truth is the rate of most cancers has actually decreased at the same time that roundup use skyrocketed.  There just isn't any real evidence that roundup actually causes cancer. Non-hodgkins lymphoma is one of the few cancers that has increased, but not dramatically, and researchers agree that the increase is almost certainly due to an increase in obesity rates.  Many of my friends are farmers who have been spraying roundup for many years, and I don't know anybody who has had non-hodgkins lymphoma. I try to be safe with the products I use for my own good and the good of my family.  I am pretty confident that glyphosate is what it was designed to be....a safe and effective way to kill weeds.  I do know that there are certainly a lot of agricultural chemicals and common household chemicals that are way more dangerous than roundup.  Stop stoking fear based on lies and misinformation.  There is no "conspiracy" regarding roundup.

Author: @rubyherring
Content: Regarding 41:36 "why would they spend so much money on ghostwritten studies if their product was safe?" - because of three things: 1. many public institutions sort out any industry funded studies because of fear that they may be biased, no matter how high their scientific quality is. 2. publication bias: if you conduct a study on a product which is generally regarded as safe and find out that it's safe, there's no real reason to publish it. It won't get you a lot of citations, so you're likely to abort the study early. So if a 100 different studies are conducted with p=0.05, then 5 of those studies will show that any given substance is carcinogenic, just as a statistical artifact. Guess which of the 100 studies will be published and which will not? Exactly. 3. who has an interest in conducting extensive safety testing? The manufacturer on the one hand, but anti-GMO-organizations or grifting scientists looking for 5 minutes of fame using bad science on the other hand. Nonpartisan academics in pursuit of the truth don't have a lot of incentive to do this - it's not exciting work, it's not cutting edge science, it's not academically prolific, and it might make you look like an industry shill. Put those three things together and you have a serious problem.

Author: @ankokuraven
Content:
Toxicology studies for regulatory submission are very often "industry funded."

It's not a red flag.  I'd be all for regulatory bodies having the funding and power to do those studies themselves, but the labs responsible for those studies are beholden to regulatory bodies, not sponsors.

I worked in toxicology for nearly a decade and have come across results for glyphosate mutagenicity and carcinogenicity testing frequently and, despite the legal cases won, have not yet seen sufficient backing for the claims.

The cancer allegations seemed to heavily tie into the public's ludicrous fears of transgenic crops.

But, as you pointed out, even taken at face value, the claimed carcinogenicity status puts it below things we consider food.  So even then, at best, this may be an issue of workplace safety for farmers, not consumers.

That said
Monsanto's business practices have always been atrocious and every allegation against those is perfectly reasonable and warranted.

Besides, there is a whole industry surrounding these court cases, involving many lawyers who may have significant financial interests in winning, given the substantial sums of money at stake.

So what I wanted to say by this, is that the carcinogenic effect on humans isn't that scientifically clear as may be stated in this video based on the scientific papers. Content:
Another aspect of Monsanto out of USA: The use of glyphosate in the war on drugs across Latin America, particularly in Colombia, has had significant negative impacts on communities, the environment, and human health. Colombia, the world's largest producer of cocaine, implemented aerial fumigation with glyphosate as part of Plan Colombia starting in 2000, a program backed by the United States This policy has led to widespread displacement of communities, especially Afro-Colombian and indigenous groups, as coca cultivation is pushed into more remote and ecologically sensitive areas like primary forests The displacement has been described as a "balloon effect," where eradication in one area leads to the expansion of coca production elsewhere, without a net reduction in cultivation

The herbicide has caused severe health problems for local populations, including skin rashes, respiratory distress, and miscarriages A 2013 study confirmed that exposure to glyphosate spraying increased the likelihood of these health issues The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classified glyphosate as a "probable carcinogen" in 2015, further raising concerns about its long-term health effects Despite this, the Colombian government has struggled to provide an effective complaint mechanism, with 93.5% of 2,265 complaints about spraying-related harm rejected between 2001 and 2015

Environmental damage is also extensive. Glyphosate drifts beyond target areas, destroying food crops, native vegetation, and aquatic ecosystems It has contributed to deforestation and biodiversity loss, particularly in critical regions like the Amazon The herbicide has even crossed international borders, prompting Ecuador to sue Colombia at the International Court of Justice over environmental damage, resulting in a $15 million settlement in 2013—though affected communities in Colombia have never received compensation

In response to mounting evidence and pressure, Colombia suspended its aerial spraying program in 2015 after the WHO's classification The suspension was reaffirmed in 2022 when the government, under President Gustavo Petro, formally ended the practice, marking a significant shift in policy Petro has called for an international pact to protect the Amazon, arguing that the war on drugs has hindered climate protection and perpetuated violence However, despite these policy changes, the legacy of glyphosate use continues to affect communities, and the debate over effective, humane, and sustainable drug policies remains ongoing

Roundup Toxicity

Excellent work: just adding that the danger of Roundup extends beyond its active ingredient, glyphosate, due to the presence of toxic adjuvants in its formulations  Commercial Roundup products contain various additives, known as adjuvants, which are not inert and can be toxic on their own  A commonly used adjuvant is the surfactant polyethoxylated tallow amine (POEA), which enhances glyphosate's effectiveness by improving its ability to wet plant surfaces and penetrate plant cuticles  However, POEA is more toxic to aquatic organisms like fish and amphibians than glyphosate alone and is not approved for use in aquatic environments  Experimental evidence shows that complete formulations, including Roundup, are often significantly more toxic to human cells and living mammals than glyphosate alone, with some studies indicating up to 1000 times greater toxicity  This increased toxicity is attributed to adjuvants like POEA, which increase the bioavailability of glyphosate and can cause severe health effects such as liver and kidney damage, respiratory distress, and even death following deliberate overdose of concentrated formulations  Regulatory assessments have historically focused only on the active ingredient, glyphosate, neglecting the potential risks posed by the full formulation, including its co-formulants  This fundamental flaw means that the long-term safety of the complete Roundup formulation has never been adequately tested or assessed.

Author: @Scinquisitor
Content:
As a biologist and a big fan of Derek I was actually disappointed with this video. I'm no fan on Monsanto, but this video contains a very one-sided story. Just to give you an example, from this video you will be very certain that glyphosate is carcinogenic. For comparison I will give you a response from ChatGPT, to the very simple prompt "Is glyphosate carcinogenic". This response is good because it covers different types of evidence and gives a reconciled conclusion. It happens to match my assessment (I studied this topic in detail once).   

Chat GPT wrote:

This is a good and tricky question — the answer depends on which scientific authority you ask and what kind of evidence they prioritize.

Here’s the state of knowledge:

🧪 Evidence & Assessments

IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer, WHO arm, 2015):
Classified glyphosate as “probably carcinogenic to humans” (Group 2A).
This was based on:

“Limited” evidence in humans (mainly studies of agricultural workers showing a possible link with non-Hodgkin lymphoma).

“Sufficient” evidence in animals (some rodent studies showing tumors).

Strong evidence of DNA and chromosomal damage in cells exposed to glyphosate.

Regulatory agencies (U.S. EPA, EFSA in Europe, Health Canada, etc.):
They reviewed more studies (including unpublished industry toxicology data) and concluded that glyphosate is unlikely to be carcinogenic to humans at real-world exposure levels.

Recent large studies:

The Agricultural Health Study (long-term, >50,000 pesticide applicators in the U.S.) found no significant overall increase in cancer risk from glyphosate, but some debate remains about non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

Meta-analyses since 2019 suggest a small possible increase in risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma among highly exposed individuals, but results are inconsistent.

⚖ How to reconcile?

IARC looked at hazard (“can it cause cancer under some circumstances?”).

Regulators focus on risk (“is it likely to cause cancer at the doses people are actually exposed to in food or environment?”).

So:

At high, repeated occupational exposures, there’s concern about a cancer link.

For the general population’s dietary exposures, most regulators currently judge the risk as very low to negligible.

✅ Bottom line: Glyphosate is possibly carcinogenic at high exposures, but typical consumer exposure (via food residues, for example) is considered unlikely to cause cancer by most regulatory agencies.

Content: OK, it's been nearly 45 years since Reagan's first term in office, so it's no surprise this key change in university funding has been forgotten. "Let's have industry pay and save tax-payer's the burden of funding universities" was the mantra used to sell this opening of the floodgates of research corruption. At the time this horror was being sold to the voting public, there were a LOT of academics and legal experts that warned this was accelerate research corruption in industry (the prime examples of the time were cigarettes, leaded gasoline, and DDT). This was exasperated by changes that privatized research journal publication (previously a non-profit activity funded by universities and taxes).

Content: I knew a guy that probably died from using Roundup concentrate. When we were teens we worked at a nursery that his father managed. We'd use it throughout the season, getting it on our hands when mixing in backpack sprayers. Now, I grew up learning about hazardous materials handling with my dad because he hauled hazardous waste and I'd sneak along. They laughed at the 16 year old me and said I was only in danger if I was a plant. Still, I figured if it killed plants, it could potentially still be harmful and rinsed my hands off after getting it on me. The other guy, let's call him John Freeman Jr., started there at 15 my first year and was a year younger than me. He was a typical lazy teenager, but by the end of the year we whipped into the our chosen nursery crew. By the end of my second season I'd injured myself and left because I was physically unable to do my job and he got my position of nursery assistant foreman. A few years had gone by, the owner screwed up and bankrupted the once world renowned century old company. I ran into one of the guys and asked what John was up to. After the nursery closed, he became a truck driver, got married and had a baby girl he adored. Then, one week he got home and told his wife he really didn't feel good. She took him to the hospital he was in such bad shape. They ran tests and found he had fully metastasized stage four cancer everywhere. He died two weeks later at only 23 years old. A few years after hearing about him, Roundup was being connected to NHL and I immediately thought of him.

Author: @Nomusicincluded
Content:
Just a few things that stuck out to me during the video. I enjoy a good discussion so feel free to push back if you disagree. As a disclaimer, I am in no way a fan of how our current agricultural system functions and I think it needs an overhaul:

1. When using internal emails as proof please keep in mind that if your job is to ensure the outcome of a paper is positive, you need to sell that to the people who are paying your salary. So are you going to write "yeah I basically did nothing and it turned out great" or are you going to oversell your work and say "yeah it was a really hard battle, but we managed to get them to change their paper." You are paid to get specific results which is an unfortunate side of our weird end-stage capitalist system, gotta love KPIs!

2. It is not just the EPA that has classified glyphosate as non-carcinogenic. Environmental agencies around the globe have as well. I want to know what is true and what is not, otherwise I will be a conspiracy theorist tomorrow. So for now I will trust that the majority of environmental agencies are not trying to kill me. 

3. Why are you using RT news to discredit Monsanto, there must be better sources out there right? I wouldn't usually suggest turning to propaganda to support an argument.

4. Why is it that we fixed on one or two products and ignore others like Copper sulphate, which is used widely in organic agriculture (you know that agricultural system that often claims it doesn't use pesticide) and may also cause cancer and may be killing bees but there is not enough scientific evidence to support an EPA finding on it.  

4. A question from my side to anyone who might know. If you control the temperature of the reaction for 2,4,D at 170, is the final product free of dioxin? Would it then be safe?

5. Academia has been infiltrated by from every side with money from businesses because we have an academic system that needs money to fund their publication and maintain a reputation (a system I absolutely hate). You want to know about supplements, well get ready for industry funded papers, how about information on organic products, well hold on to your hats, medicine? Good luck... This is the unfortunate reality of our academic space, and honestly I am not sure what the solution is. 

Finally one note to those talking about the drinking glyphosate interview. I know it is great sensationalist fodder but the reality is we use many products that we would not consume an entire cup of during an interview, try dry coffee, capsaicin, salt, wasabi, ipecac... I know I am fun at parties.
