Content:
Thank you for making these very important videos such as the Pfoas one and this one about Monsanto. About the section on Agent Orange in Vietnam War, I would like to add a few things : 

1) It is said in the video that Monsanto and other companies knew of the toxicity of agent orange and did not tell the US government. It feels implied that the US is unaware of the toxicity when it used it during Ranch Hand operation and it feels implied that the government is a victim of the deception of Monsanto and others. I hope people don't do this implication shortcut. Indeed, your video says that the scientific petition happened in 1967 to condemn the use of agent orange. The US still continued to use agent orange until 1970-1971. Which means that even though they knew the concerns about it, they still continued. So we don't know actually if the government knew about this even before or not. Especially when there were other projects already in the 1940-1950 to study the use of this chemical in warfare by the military...And especially when the  Kimmig & Schulz studies were publicly published in 1957, the results were not only sent in private letters to companies.

2) It is not that clear that the origin idea of defoliating the jungle comes only from Ngo Dinh Diem, even though he strongly approved of it, and thus have a part of responsibility in the aftermath. Indeed the US were already very involved in the South government of Vietnam....in fact they were already very involved in the Indochina war helping the French already in the 1950s with military help and advice. And knowing that there were already projects on the use of defoliants in warfare by the US, the situation is a bit more complex than just Ngo Dinh Diem asking the US for defoliation help. There is a strong intention from the US government to frame everything in the conflict as an internal conflict, an internal war and making sure that the US has minimal responsibility in the aftermath. But when looking at how much they were involved in reality, the acts done, it is not as they say.

3) Even though mostly victims being sprayed are by accident, meaning the people are not the spraying targets in the first place. When such a large amount of land is sprayed, it is not surprising that there are actual people living on these lands and if not then there are soldiers from both sides who will almost surely be sprayed. And then there's even the contamination of water source, contamination of soil.

4) Several attempts by Vietnamese victims at suing either the companies producing the defoliants (Monsanto, Dow...) or the US government in the decision to spray them were all unsuccessful. Fortunately, the US veterans and Korean veterans have been heard and are being compensated for their victims. But the largest number of victims in Vietnam, mostly are now children of people exposed to the poison, they didn't find this justice. The latest known suing case is from Mrs Tran To Nga against all these chemical giants in 2024 . We really should get monsanto and dow to face up for the sins of dioxin.

Content:
Oh boy, here we go 🙄 The reason why you and the public don't understand the problem with the IARC classification is because you don't understand the difference between a hazard and a risk.

A hazard is something that may cause harm to you. Risk is a combination of the hazard and a probability that said hazard will actually harm you (risk = hazard x probability).

The classification of IARC is flawed because it says nothing about risk, it only classifies a "potential" hazard. 

Glyphosate is thus in group 2A of IARC. Do you know what else is there? Eating red meat, drinking beverages hotter than 65°C, acrylamide which is formed when you cook at high temperatures, night shift work (yes, disrupting your circadian rythm is classified as a hazard potentially leading to cancer).

Furthermore, the European Food Safety Agency, which arguably is the foremost agency in the world, has conducted and analysed many studies, even after the IARC classification, and the conclusion was the same as before. When used correctly, the exposure farmers and the public get to glyphosate is unlikely to lead to cancer.

Author: @TheDoc73
Content:
I never considered the mechanism of glyphosate interacting with your gut microbiom, but it now makes sense why it specifically can cause non-hodgkin's lymphoma.

Among the many things lymphocytes do in the body is of course phagocytosis. This means the lymphocyte, I believe specifically NKT cells, surrounds the bacteria and destroys it within its own cytoplasm. A process which results in everything inside that bacteria being left inside that lymphocyte. Glyphosate might have no impact on our cells, but putting raw cellular material from glyphosate-exposed bacteria inside your lymphocytes might be able to affect their DNA.

I'm not an expert by any means, but if you want to prove the link between glyphosate and cancer in a lab, that's where I'd look. I'd look at NKT cells eating exposed bacteria and record the rate at which they become cancerous.

Author: @meiliodinson
Content:
I feel like this is a case of Streisand effect. Glyphosate and even 2,4-D by themselves (without any by-products), while not 100% safe, aren't particularly dangerous or carcinogenic for humans. However, the aggressive, predatory, mafia-like behaviour of the company towards farmers and their effort to silence any evidence, however small and inconsequential, that the product had any harmful effect—well, that only made it more visible and backfired on them. They could just have accepted the IRAC study knowing full well that their classification is based on the mechanism, not risk. They would have been fine acknowledging it, same with many other potential carcinogens that we still use because there is just no better alternative and the benefits outweigh the dangers (although not the best example, you could throw out meat in there, as cited in the video). But they saw it as a threat and their "let nothing go" policy—clearly motivated by a desire to maximize profit—made them act irrationally (or rationally, for capitalist agents?), which led to all this mess. Which is a shame because the molecules by themselves are pretty useful (and reasonably safe if care is awarded to at-risk individuals like farmers).

The main culprit is, as always, the system in which these molecules were used: capitalism. Allowing molecules to be patented and monopolies in so-called free markets, and besides that, not having enough safeguards to prevent interference in academic, scientific and judicial bodies by rich companies—this is the big scandal everyone should be worried about, and it is affecting so much more than this particular case.

We could also question the need for herbicides at all: even a theorical 100% safe herbicide for humans (and our microbiome) would still have negative consequences for the environment, but once again, capitalism makes it essential to structure our agriculture this way. It's a common theme, really: we profit now, and we ignore what negative consequences might arise in a few decades. From an outside perspective, the USA seems a pretty lost cause in this but I'm still hopeful capitalism being on its dying bed right now might lead to a change of system, because honestly capitalism is poisoning every aspects of our lives, not just some weed.

Author: @IVIune
Content:
This often gets framed as 'glyphosate = bad' or 'glyphosate = safe,' which misses the key scientific principle: the dose makes the poison.

Even water is lethal if you consume a massive dose in a short period. The LD50 (the lethal dose for 50% of test subjects) for water is about 90 ml/kg. For glyphosate, it's about 5,600 ml/kg. This means, by sheer volume, you need to ingest over 60 times more glyphosate than water to reach a lethal dose.

The real question isn't 'is it poison?'—everything is in a high enough dose. The question is, 'are the trace residues found in food or the exposure levels for farmers high enough to significantly increase cancer risk?' That's where the scientific debate truly lies, and it's a much more complex issue.

Author: @segurahx
Content:
00:00 The Murder of Farmer Mike Wallace

• Farmer Mike Wallace from Arkansas was murdered because of a herbicide owned by the Monsanto company.
• The herbicide sowed fear among farmers, turning them against each other.

00:42 The Monsanto Monopoly

• Monsanto had a monopoly on farmland, controlling more than 80% of the seeds in the United States.
• The company used the legal system and corrupt officials to gain a monopoly.

01:31 The Discovery of Herbicide

• Chemist Franklin D. Jones was looking for a way to get rid of poison ivy by spraying it with hormones.
• The growth hormone 2,4-D caused the ivy to grow uncontrollably and die.

03:05 Selective herbicides

• 2,4-D killed broadleaf weeds but did not damage crops.
• Adding chlorine to the benzene ring increased the selectivity of the herbicide.

04:06 Industrial production of herbicides

• Herbicides replaced manual methods of weed control.
• Monsanto patented selective herbicides in 1945.

05:16 Explosion at the Monsanto plant

• In 1949, an explosion occurred at the Monsanto plant in Nitro, West Virginia.
• ​​Workers became ill, their skin was covered with rashes and pustules.

07:47 Research by Karl Schulz

• German dermatologist Karl Schulz discovered a link between work at Monsanto plants and skin diseases.
• Schultz tested herbicide ingredients on rabbit ears and had no reaction.

09:50 Dioxin Formation

• Dioxin was formed when the heat was raised during the herbicide production process.

• Schultz tested dioxin-contaminated TCP on himself and experienced the same symptoms as the workers at the plant.

10:40 Dioxin Warning

• Schultz contacted German chemical manufacturers.
• German company warns Monsanto and Dow of dioxin contamination.
• Monsanto denies receiving letters, Dow claims they were mixed up.

11:27 The Vietnam War and Operation Ranch Hand

• In 1961, South Vietnam asked the United States for help in the war against the Viet Cong.
• The United States sent herbicides, including Agent Orange.
• Agent Orange destroyed 20% of the jungle, but was toxic to humans and animals.

13:02 Consequences of Agent Orange

• By 1965, it was clear that dioxin was a threat.
• The US sprayed 72 million liters of Agent Orange, which contained 80 liters of dioxin.
• Civilians and soldiers suffered from skin diseases and cancer, children were born with physical and mental disabilities.

13:52 Public reaction and Monsanto research

• In 1967, scientists signed a petition against the use of herbicides.
• Monsanto looked for a replacement for 245 tons, but after nine years of research, they achieved nothing.

14:33 Discovery of glyphosate

• John E. Franz tested 19 possible herbicides.
• The second herbicide was ten times more powerful than the others.
• Glyphosate blocked the shikimate pathway in plants, killing them.

16:53 The benefits of glyphosate

• Glyphosate affected an enzyme in plants, but not humans or animals.
• Microorganisms in the soil broke down glyphosate into harmless byproducts.
• In 1974, Monsanto released Roundup.

18:28 Monsanto's monopoly on glyphosate

• By the late 1980s, Monsanto was selling 7 million pounds of Roundup and earning a billion dollars a year.
• Glyphosate was patented, giving Monsanto a monopoly.

19:16 The problem of Roundup resistance

• Roundup killed all plants, including crops.
• Monsanto tried to make crops resistant to Roundup, but it didn’t work.

21:33 Genetic engineering and glyphosate resistance

• Monsanto scientists isolated a genetic sequence from Salmonella that changed the shape of the EPSPS enzyme, making it resistant to glyphosate.
• Salmonella DNA was placed in a gene gun and fired into plant tissue at 100 km/h.
• Gold particles with DNA were bombarded into plant cells, and some of them were integrated into the plant’s chromosomes.

22:20 Resistant seeds succeed

• Seeds with the new genes were planted in a field and sprayed with Roundup, but nothing happened — the soybeans were resistant.
• By 1998, Monsanto had patented glyphosate-resistant canola, corn, and cotton, calling them “Roundup-ready.” • By 2001, more than 70% of soybeans in the United States were grown using Monsanto seeds, and Roundup had become the top-selling agricultural product.

23:03 Monsanto Agreement Terms

• Farmers signed agreements requiring them not to save or sell seeds derived from Monsanto seeds.
• Farmers had to identify Monsanto and allow Monsanto representatives access to land for research.
• Signing the agreement or opening a seed packet automatically accepted the terms of the agreement.

26:07 Farmer Control

• Monsanto controlled the market by threatening farmers with bankruptcy if they did not sign agreements.
• The company used private investigators, former police officers, and pilots to inspect farms.
• There was a hotline for reporting neighbors who violated the agreements.

28:37 Farmer Consequences

• By 2013, Monsanto had sued more than 400 farmers, earning more than $20 million.
• Many farmers went bankrupt or settled out of court.
• A culture of fear and paranoia turned neighbors against each other.

30:28 Farm Tragedy

• Mike Wallace suspected that herbicide from a neighboring farm had destroyed his soybeans. • Tensions between farms led to a row in which a farm worker shot and killed Wallace.
• Similar tragedies have occurred around the world where Monsanto has infiltrated farming communities

31:56 IARC Classification of Glyphosate

• The US Environmental Protection Agency EPA and the World Health Organization WHO maintain that glyphosate does not pose a carcinogenic risk.
• IARC has classified glyphosate as a probable carcinogen, which has come as a surprise to the public.
• Monsanto has expressed dissatisfaction with the IARC's decision and demanded that it be corrected.

33:03 Brent Wisner's Investigation Begins

• California lawyer Brent Wisner has become interested in the link between Roundup and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.
• He has teamed up with other lawyers and an investigative journalist to investigate Monsanto.

34:08 Lawsuit and Access to Documents

• A group of lawyers filed a lawsuit against Monsanto and gained access to its internal documents.
• The documents showed the company's duplicity and deception.

34:44 Glyphosate Research and Classification

• In 1983, Monsanto presented the results of a toxicology study on glyphosate that showed rare kidney tumors in mice.
• The EPA demanded more studies, but Monsanto resisted.
• In 1991, the EPA classified glyphosate as having evidence of non-carcinogenicity in humans.

36:15 Independent Studies and Their Criticisms

• A 2000 paper by Williams, Croos, and Monroe concluded that Roundup was safe.
• However, the paper was not independent, as Monsanto's toxicology director, William Heydens, was listed as a scientific consultant.

37:19 Monsanto's manipulation

• Monsanto tried to change the classification of glyphosate and colluded with corrupt EPA officials.
• In 2017, Wisner released internal Monsanto documents revealing manipulation schemes.

38:01 Public reaction and lawsuits

• Cancer patients who used Roundup began filing lawsuits against Monsanto.
• By the end of the year, more than 3,000 victims had joined the case.

38:41 Monsanto's strategy and its consequences

• Monsanto used a "leave nothing behind" strategy to discredit opponents.
• The company conducted training for nutritionists and scientists to teach them how to properly talk about glyphosate.

40:10 Bayer Acquires Monsanto


41:25 Roundup Dangers

• Monsanto Denies Roundup Link to Cancer

• IARC Considers Glyphosate Genotoxic

• Excessive Glyphosate Exposure Can Damage Cell DNA

42:22 Impact on the Microbiome

• Glyphosate Can Disrupt the Gut Microbiome

• Disruption of EPSP Synthase Enzyme Can Have Various Effects

42:33 Classification of Carcinogens

• IARC Classifies Glyphosate as a Probable Carcinogen

• Other Carcinogens: Red Meat, High-Temperature Frying, Night Shift Work, Alcohol, Tobacco, Sunlight

• PFOA Is a Classified Carcinogen

43:22 Risks and Controversy

• Increased glyphosate exposure is associated with a modest increase in cancer risk.
• The EPA and others disagree with IARC.
• U.S. courts criticize agency for insufficient analysis.

44:04 Research Funding

• About 50% of glyphosate safety studies have been funded by industry.
• Companies seek to control science.

44:27 Bayer's Position

• Bayer denies glyphosate is carcinogenic.
• The company has removed glyphosate from commercial products due to backlash and lawsuits.
• Weed resistance to glyphosate is growing.

45:27 Protecting Sensitive People

• It is important to protect the most sensitive people from glyphosate exposure.

45:41 Monsanto's Influence on Science

• Monsanto Manipulates Research Results.
• Rules are needed to ensure the independence of science.

46:30 Recommendations 

• Recommended books: The Monsanto Papers by Carrie Gill and Start-up Capital by Bart Elmore.

Content: Monsanto is a horrible company, and absolutely is to blame for dioxin poisonings as well as for patent witch hunts. The reason why Monsanto had to fend off endless lawsuits, well it's pretty clear when you  consider everything else they've done that they've lost in the court of opinion. Your average person is neutral to anti GMO at baseline, partly due to this companies actions and gross misunderstanding. GMO crops have raised farming productivity massively, which makes food cheap, and while the 1st world could still eat without them, the 3rd would struggle. Billions of lives depend on productive farming, and now that roundup ready is off patent, it can finally be cheaper and more accessible. The power of genetic engineering is better and more accessible every year, I only hope that leads to new innovations that may one day allow the average farmer to make his own GMO crops. Knowledge ought to be freely shared, these patents are actively stifling competition.

Author: @mxyplex
Content:
Even if the maximum adi of glyphosate would cause cancer, you'd have to look at the relative risk of that dose. For glyphosate that would be 3-6 (3-6/50 vs 1-2/50 for control) at 10000x the adi. If this scares you, you might want to consider not breathing air. 

There's also the amount of food one would need to consume to reach this amount. For example the highest tested and found trace of glyphosate in any food would need you to consume 4kg of it to reach that limit, and for it to have an effect you'd have to do it daily, over a long time. Consumers are reported at <10% consumed of the adi. If you do the math on this you would need to consume 17metric tons a day to get to a 3-6RR. 

IARC only tells you if something is a carcinogen, at any dose, which is true for glyphosate, and for a lot of things you put in your body daily. But no one has ever proved that, not even close, at the consumer level. 

The adi in EU is set at a low dose, with a 100x-10000x buffer where at 100x the RR is 1.0. This is what the EU does, in general, for all things approved for food. The studies and science behind this doesn't add up, unless you're claiming a massive global conspiracy that everyone who works for any food safety agency is in on it. 

Monsanto has done a lot of really awful things, obviously. But if you're gonna make a video looking into science you should probably include all the science, and try to explain it.

This was highly biased and poorly presented at the end. All this does it fuel conspiracy and anti establishment.

Author: @frankbarajas
Content: In the early 90's I was weeding my yard of my first house with Round-Up on a windy day and when I turned the corner of my house a gust of wind pushed the spray into my face. I inhaled some of it and some got in my eyes but the effects didn't seem serious, just an irritation like shampoo in your eyes during a shower. Then about six weeks later I started suffering severe pain in my chest, and after seeing a doctor, undergoing various tests, they discovered a small ulcer in my esophagus. It took about six months being treated with meds but eventually the area healed and the pain when away. Then in 2022 I had a kidney stone and during that course of treatment they found a golf ball size tumor on my kidney. While I can't say the two events have any connection, it is the only time I used Round-Up and were it not for tiny 2mm kidney stone I wouldn't be here today. However, I still wonder what gave me that kidney tumor and probably always will wonder if we are truly safe or merely walking through a minefield planted with some greedy corporation's GMOs and Chemicals?

Author: @omaclean
Content:
Video was dissapointingly thin on the data of the impact of glyphosate. The best we got was "moderate risk increase for certain specific cancers".

The best data I can find is "Non Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) relative risk : 1.41 with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.13 to 1.75." but the effect couldn't be found in a subsequent dataset.

Now, the dose impacts might vary, but that means if we take that best 1.41 estimate: if three farmers with NHL sued Monsanto for their cancer, on average two of their cancers would not have been caused by glyphosate.

Paradoxically, Monsanto's strangulation of the narrative and research may have hurt them. By restricting research they are now left with such noisy data, making it easier for their opposing lawyers to point at circumstantial evidence like "why would they spend money if they have nothing to hide". Which is weak evidence for such a normally good scientific channel to focus on instead of proper scientific analyses.

Author: @antares4141
Content:
Interesting video! While the evidence that 2,4,5-T contained dioxin and that this caused a plethora of health conditions is clear, the same is still not clear for glyphosate, is it? Didn't Bayer settle as a business decision, not as an admission to the claims levied against it?

If litigants were users of the product—meaning they got their exposure the same way hundreds of millions of other users did—except they got cancer where the hundreds of millions of other users apparently did not, does that mean they got it from glyphosate?

Does  Roundup Ready corn or soy pose a risk?  Since the spraying is done very early when crops are seedlings, not when they are full-grown plants, giving them a lot of time to shed any residue. The opposite would seem to be true in the practice of desiccation, where farmers spray non-GMO wheat and soy a week or two before harvest so that it is dry or desiccated when it is sold. There, the crop is clearly covered with glyphosate when it is shipped off to be processed.

And while someone can argue, 'we don't know it's bad for you,' common sense would dictate that you want to limit (reasonably) your exposure to a chemical like this, whether it can be proved to be bad or not. People should be complaining about this, not GMOs!

And since we are essentially using ourselves as guinea pigs with the wheat desiccation experiment, we should conduct studies on ourselves. Data should be collected and analyzed for safety. You have to keep in mind we are trying to feed 8 billion people, and we need to use every tool we have responsibly. This means using things like glyphosate if it can be shown to be reasonably safe.

Content:
Long Post -
Haven't watched the entire vid, ( because I know Monsanto is a sticky subject ) but, I've read quite a few comments, so here's my take on the "Monsanto conspiracy."
The real problem with Monsanto is that just like other multinationals like Raytheon, Phizer and Exxon Mobil, is its position at the tip of the spear of something people know is an existential threat to all humanity, but cannot explain why, because it goes deep into biotechnology, but also intersects serious ethical and moral issues.
Long story short, the average farmer doesn't understand how plant hormones such as cytokinin, gibberellic acid, auxins and meristematic cells work, but  they certainly understand pretty darn  well, how agro - economics work, because for them, that's what pays the bills.
Enter the " Monsanto conspiracies ".
Up to about two decades ago, farmers had options in plant materials aka, "germplasm" ( seeds etc ) from various companies to cultivate varieties that suited the markets, netting them top dollars. Monsanto now controls ALL seed production, globally, using a vertically integrated business model.
What can possibly go wrong there?
In terms of biotechnology, Monsanto controls ALL research globally.
Again, what could possibly go wrong?
To fully understand, do some research on farmers suicide in India linked to BT cotton and bringal ( eggplant ) production in India. BT cotton was basically the first foray into a bio - engineered  crop production in the USA. India was used as the guinea pig to test the efficacy of the specific cultivar of cotton seeds engineered with a specific toxin ( Bacillus Thurengiensis ) designed to sterilize and kill the larvae of an insect that destroy the cotton plant. While the technology was a massive success for the farmer, the problem came when they tried to plant the seeds after their first harvest.
None of the seeds produced cotton, because the parent company that did the seeds basically patented the seeds by also manipulating the genetic structure of the plant to produce sterile seeds. Because the farmers were sold on the idea of higher yeilds with the BT coton seeds from the USA, many of them borrowed huge sums of money to purchase the F1 ( first gen. hybrid ) seeds, hoping to sell the cotton and replant the seeds, thus, making a profit.
Because the second gen seeds were engineered to be sterile, many farmers were unable to pay their debt, and committed "self deletion."
Therein lies the real problem with Monsanto.
Another example in the USA is Monsanto's production of corn called "Roundup Ready Corn." Just like the BT cotton in India, the active ingrediant in the weedkiller " Roundup", glyphosate ammonia, is enginnered into the corn to make it resistant to weedkillers containing glyphosate..The immediate effect is, higher production yeilds for farmers, because they no longer have to spend tons on money on selective weedkillerd for corn .( which are expensive ). Author: @ags1917-p1i
Content:
Veritasium’s video did not engage with the reasons cited by multiple government agencies that consider glyphosate safe. In addition, most of the featured pundits appear to be either lawyers involved in litigation seeking about $10 billion in damages or authors who have profited from criticizing Monsanto.

One key regulator, EFSA (European Food Safety Authority), regularly bans substances it deems a priori safer than Roundup—including flufenacet, a top-selling herbicide banned as recently as 2024. In fact, the core guideline for EFSA and ECHA is the precautionary principle: "an approach to risk management, where, if it is possible that a given policy or action might cause harm to the public or the environment and if there is still no scientific agreement on the issue, the policy or action in question should not be carried out". This has created one of the safest environments for consumers in history. The authors either ignore this principle or willingly have decided to hide it. 

Despite all that context, the video’s only “safety assessment” was a pundit’s assertion that glyphosate “increases modestly the chances of getting cancer,” followed by a claim that overuse “definitely increases risk,” without presenting data to support either statement. Some research supporting those claims would have been welcomed.

For reference, the most recent risk assessments from EFSA and ECHA (2023) were issued after reviewing thousands of submissions and allegations (some emerging after court cases involving Monsanto/Bayer). Those assessments note, among other points:

“Studies reporting effects on microbiome were considered and taken into account for the risk assessment in the areas of mammalian toxicology and ecotoxicology. Currently, no internationally agreed guidelines for the risk assessment of microbiome are in place in the pesticide area. Further research in the field of microbiome is needed to understand its relevance for risk assessment and to develop dedicated strategies and methodologies accordingly.

Following the assessment based on the available evidence, glyphosate does not meet the criteria for endocrine disruption as laid down in points 3.6.5 and 3.8.2 of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009, as amended by Commission Regulation (EU) No 2018/605.”

(Peer review of the pesticide risk assessment of the active substance glyphosate - available via EFSA’s online library.)

I’m not trying to play devil’s advocate; I was genuinely hoping for a full, in-depth, evidence-based investigation that weighed regulatory findings alongside contrary claims. What I found? A disappointing tale about good vs evil that does not address the full complexity of the issue.

Author: @nichtrichtigrum
Content:
Thanks to the Veritasium team for drawing attention to this! I loved the video!

I want to add that the environmental impacts of Agent Orange and Roundup were (or are) also horrible. In Vietnam, forests largely still haven't recovered with chemicals estimated to persist in the ground for ca. 100 years. With Roundup, Monsanto helped shape modern agriculture, so that it's now almost completely monocultures. Without anything else growing there, not even a weed here and there, many animals like insects or rodents can't survive. Insects dying is also a great concern for us humans because we lose a lot of pollinators that we need to grow a lot of food.

During the time of the Monsanto acquisition by Bayer, I was active at Greenpeace in Germany, and despite these huge impacts on the environment, Greenpeace Germany stayed completely quiet when all the media was talking about Monsanto. I suggested to organize some sort of protest before the acquisition. I was then told that Greenpeace HQ had decided there would be no actions concerning Monsanto this year. I have the strong suspicion that someone at Greenpeace HQ was threatened or bribed. I started only supporting small NGOs after that.

Agricultural companies like Monsanto lobby against sustainable (not necessarily GMO-free, just sustainable) farming practices and through promotion and affordable pricing of crops mainly used for animal feed (like soy or corn), they help keep meat artificially cheap, driving an unsustainable expansion of agriculture. To make our agriculture more sustainable, we need regulations that not only aim at protecting the consumers but the environment, too, regardless, if it has been domestically produced or imported. A tax on meat or land use or a tax on produce coming from deforested areas would help a lot.

If you also think, this is important, maybe tell a friend about this topic.

Author: @Themax342
Content:
It gets even worse than this.
I did a presentation about Monsanto in Highschool. 
This was back in 2014 and I was supposed to show how starvation occurred around the planet. 
I very quickly learned that it’s possible to genetically modify seeds to be able to consume way less water than usual, so they would be able to grow in very dry areas and also have a higher yield. 
Monsanto had all the patents for these seeds. 
So everyone who needed them back then was forced to buy from Monsanto. Thanks to the modification these plants would not even grow seeds themselves so there was no need for any dubious contracts. 
When you overlayed a map with starvation deaths per population and a map with seeds sold by Monsanto, they would pretty much match exactly because none of the poor countries were able to pay enough for these seeds. 
So the result of my presentation was very quickly that the reason for starvation around the world was entirely down to profit maximization by Monsanto and not lack of wealth, overpopulation or difficult climate. 
That’s why I was horrified and confused as a German when Bayer bought Monsanto because these tactics should not be possible under eu law. But I have no Idea if it’s still the same today.

Edit: just to be clear this is just a correlation and not necessary causation. I don't remember my exact sources but it was pretty clear that it was a causation because Monsanto legally had the only seeds that were able to grow in dry regions and they didn't sell them in regions where starvation occured.
The core problem is of course still poverty in individual countries or among farmers because with more money they could afford these seeds.
But don't take this as fact, it was in highschool 11 years ago.

Content: When it comes right down to it Monsanto was an evil corporation with evil intent and an army of corporate lawyers. The foremost intent was to corner the soybean and corn seed markets by any means necessary. Farmers were forced to either pay Monsanto or destroy thousand of acres of viable crops unknowingly cross pollinated with Monsanto's strains. Thus began the slow demise of private farms and the rise of corporate owned big agriculture. Because Monsanto in their seed contracts with farmers (no you cannot just walk into a store and buy it you need a seed contract) forbid them keeping any of the resulting seeds from Monsanto's strains and reusing them. Now that the Monsanto patent on their genetically modified original products has passed there still remains the cross pollination of crops. Quite a few countries refuse to allow the products from the genetically modified strains to be imported into their countries due to those genetic modifications. Another evil Monsanto and big corn agriculture propagated was to get American foodstuff makers to switch to Corn Syrup instead of using Cane Sugar. While all that was going on Monsanto and Big Agriculture convinced (bribed) congress critters to force automobile fuel makers to spike the automobile fuel with ethanol made from corn. Claiming falsely that it would help alleviate some environmental issues with the then standard automobile fuel.  This caused many problems forcing auto makers, worldwide, to reengineer their cars engine fuel systems so that the ethanol would not break down hoses, gaskets and rubber O Rings. The side products made from corn and soybeans are very pervasive. Including animal feed, plastics, fuel, and human foodstuffs. HOWEVER, ironically, because we've tilled our soils to death, no till is becoming important in Europe. People do what's called direct sowing in cover crops, a step beyond the "normal" no-till. In regular no till, you do nothing between crops, you just spray, and you seed. In cover crop farming, you grow beneficial plants between two crops, you roll them over when they flower, killing them, you sow into that. If you got a "normal" soil, quite rich, and your cover crops is dense, everything grows fine. BUT since our soils are so poor after decades of tilling, it's mostly tough perennial weeds that grow, and only glyphosate can calm them down. Without glypho, your yield is poor. There are some inovation in the "rolling over" step, with rollers that can shear perennials heavily, but they're not as full proof as glyphosate sadly... And if you don't use glypho, in organic farming ? They till to remove the weed. So they destroy their soils even faster, like in Spain. So you have a niche where glyphosate can help the transition to restoring soil health, which is very ironic... And those farmers are afraid about the glyphosate ban that's coming,  because the alternative herbicides are worse... 

Oh and by the way, those GMO crops are HORRIBLE. They are weaker than their non-GMO counterparts, so need MORE pesticides, against fungi and insect attack. So although GMO products are not dangerous to eat IN THEMSELVEs, they come from farms that use a lot more chemicals than other farms, simply because they're growing a much weaker plant that need more chemical help to survive... Author: @Jay-b4j4w
Content:
How is Monsanto still alive and kicking? This company should’ve been dismantled half a century ago. Instead, it merged into Bayer, slapped on a new mask, and kept running the same poison racket: glyphosate, PFAS, heavy metals, GMOs, dumped into our food, our water, our soil, and our bodies.

Glyphosate (Roundup) is systemic. It doesn’t rinse off, it’s pulled into the DNA of the plant. That means it’s in your oats, corn, wheat, chips, popcorn, tobacco, even so-called “organic” grains. Court cases like Johnson v. Monsanto proved the link to non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, juries awarded billions. Yet the FDA still lets it saturate the food chain. Why? Because of the revolving door.

Executives walk straight from Monsanto’s boardroom into the FDA, write the rules, then bounce back to the same company. Michael Taylor is the poster childMonsanto VP, then FDA Deputy Commissioner for Foods, literally drafting the policies that governed his former employer. That’s not oversight, that’s organized corruption. It’s like letting a prisoner become a guard, smuggling contraband, and then blaming visitors while the whole system rots.

And every few years, they quietly “adjust” the regulations—raising the “safe” limit on glyphosate, cadmium, lead, PFAS. Safe? That’s a lie. There is no safe level of poison in your body. If they think it’s safe, make them eat it. Spray Monsanto board members’ dinners until it drips, put it in their kids’ lunchboxes, and let them chew it live on camera. You’ll never see it happen, because they know the truth.

I bought a bag of USDA “organic” pumpkin seeds from Safeway. Thought I was doing my body good. Ate half the bag before noticing the Prop 65 label: known to the State of California to cause cancer, birth defects, and reproductive harm due to lead, cadmium, and other heavy metals. That’s what “organic” means in America, paperwork games and poison with a label slapped on the back. That’s not food, that’s fraud.

And it’s not just glyphosate. We’re dealing with PFAS and PFOS, forever chemicals. Created by DuPont and 3M, pushed into the world through Pioneer (Monsanto’s sister company), and now showing up in rivers, farmland, rain, even the Great Lakes. They don’t break down. They don’t flush out. They accumulate in blood and organs. The EPA itself admits there is no safe level of PFAS in drinking water. Yet here we are—drinking it every day.

This isn’t a conspiracy, it’s public record. Look it up:
 Johnson v. Monsanto (2018) – glyphosate linked to cancer.
 Michael Taylor – Monsanto VP turned FDA policymaker.
 California Proposition 65 – mandatory cancer warnings on “organic” foods.
 EPA statements on PFAS – “no safe level” in water.

America is a giant petri dish. We are guinea pigs. While you’re distracted by partisan politics, Tesla protests, and the media parroting the same scripts word-for-word, the chemical cartel keeps cashing in on your slow death.

Wake up. Stop letting the FDA act as Monsanto’s bodyguard. Demand leaders—RFK Jr., Trump, anyone with guts—to rip out this cartel by the roots and rebuild these agencies to serve the people, not the corporations. Because if we don’t, we’ll keep eating their poison while they keep moving the bar on what’s “safe”—until there’s nothing left in us worth saving.

Content: Well done, but it's a bit disappointing because a few conclusions were skipped. First, 2-4-D, even in the much maligned Agent Orange mixture, is and was always safe as long as it was free from dioxin. Second, the risk from glyphosate is proportional to exposure (if harmful at all), so PPE and safe handling are the correct responses. We accept this risk with MANY chemicals.  Third, the benefit to humanity has FAR outweighed the harm. Herbicides and lab seeds have allowed Earth to sustain human populations far beyond what would have been possible otherwise.  For the purists who believe even small risk is unacceptable, you need to quit driving cars, riding bikes, eating meat, or doing anything ever that might cause a proportional risk to you.  Lastly, the hard evidence that Monsanto manipulated reporting is concerning, but it's not evidence of product risks.  All major brands engage in marketing ploys to combat marketing against them. That, in itself, is normal business and doesn't prove or disprove any science.

Author: @smallfox8623
Content: This is a seriously disappointing video from a science channel. To be clear none of the regulatory agencies even in Europe where they tend to be more cautious have found any clear causal link between glyphosate and NHL. That’s mentioned quickly at the very end but is dismissed out of hand as essentially industry backed propaganda. An argument used at the end is “if it’s safe why do you need to spend so much on industry research and PR” and the answer should be obvious to anyone engaged in any level of critical thinking: the company was facing billions in liabilities from the courts. The courts are not a scientific body and them being critical of the procedures used at the EPA is completely irrelevant and tells us nothing about the scientific consensus. I imagine most people will come away from this video with the impression that glyphosate definitively causes NHL and any evidence to the contrary is paid for by Monsanto. That is a hilariously wrong conclusion and ironically causes significantly more harm to trust in science than just not saying anything. It’s cute how the video also preempts any criticism in the comments by suggesting Monsanto will hire shills.

The main things everyone should take away from this:
1-Bleach does not cause cancer. It is, however, not safe. If bleach was marketed as perfectly safe, we know it wouldn't hold any water against lawsuits. 3-Industries can and will use any resource at their disposal to keep testing all of their products not because they want them to be safe, but because they want more money (R+D) and, above all, they don't want fear, doubt or criticism to hurt their numbers from going up. Most of this conspiracy isn't about glyphosate, just like it wasn't about patents. It's about shareholders maybe not making as much money. No company that big will ever care about anything else. No exec, not even a middleman in a suit, was ever nay will ever face charges: they are insulated by money (and fear of accidents, iykyk).
4-You should always distrust companies. That does not mean they lie all the time, or that private research is fake. It does mean, however, that you should never assume you have the full picture. In fact, Monsanto and others (BP and Exxon are big players at that) have in the past (and currently BAYER are still doing it, afaik) infiltrated movements or even funded controlled opposition. Author: @fishyerik
Content:
The IARC  classification was largely based on the study that found increased incidence of non-hodgkin lymphoma, and the infamous Séralini study. The "non-hodgkin lymphoma study", wasn't a controlled study, it was an "observational study", looking for any kind of statistical increase in cancer, any forms of cancer, in people with occupational exposure to glyphosate, which means they were p-hacking to create "evidence", without controlling for other variables, which means they found a small correlation, not proving causality, not at all. By p-hacking enough data you can find correlation between anything and increased incidence of some form of cancer.     

The Séralini "study", the basis of what's now known as the "Séralini affair" used very small sample sizes, of Sprague Dawley rats. The thing with Sprague Dawley rats is that is a lab strain that develops huge tumors, just given time. Séralini pointed out some cherry-picked differences between "exposed" and control groups, that weren't statistically significant and showed Sprague Dawley rats with huge tumors, implying that glyphosate and GMO-corn had caused those huge tumors, but there were no significant differences between "exposed" groups and controls. 

Not that it proves anything about glyphosate, but it might be interesting to know that Séralini have published a lot of "studies" among other things claiming to prove homeopathic remedies having actual medicinal effects, besides the placebo effect.  

It's also important to remember that court rulings are not scientific proof. And whatever bad things Monsanto did a very long time ago doesn't prove anything about glyphosate.

Monsanto did sue farmers over patent infringements, that's a perfectly normal thing to do if you hold the patents for a highly powerful commercial system and commercial operators infringe on your patent. Last time I checked, Monsanto donated all the money they received from those lawsuits, a fact they weren't exactly shy about, so that's common knowledge among people that spent any time trying to objectively understand the history, you just "forgot" to mention that, huh, Derek?    

A farmer that sprays their fields with any herbicide, from any company, so recklessly that he or she kills their neighbor's crops is the problem in that situation, not the herbicide manufacturer.      

And, the huge benefits is the main reason glyphosate and roundup-ready crops took off like it did, not fear of loosing the crops due to neighbors' horrifically reckless spraying of glyphosate.  

It's completely normal that commercial seeds are covered by intellectual property protection, and farmers buying new seed instead of saving seeds, that's not unique for Monsanto, or Bayer, or "GMO"-seeds, or herbicide resistant strains. Crop strains for commercial farming are constantly improved upon, and production of those seeds needs higher level of control to have as little weed seeds and other contaminants as possible. Saving seeds from production for consumption rarely makes sense anyway, especially more than one or a few cycles, as productivity will decrease compared to buying new seeds, of the latest variants, that has been produced with higher levels of control, both regarding crop genetics, and contamination of both weed seeds and diseases.    

While an amateur, or even part time commercial grower might not even notice a 20% reduction in yield, 10% difference in yield can make the difference between good profit and bankruptcy for a "real" farmer, you know, those very few farmers that actually produce most of the food we eat.                     

While Monsanto certainly has done some really bad things, the worst of their deeds is ancient history, and don't have anything to do with, and also don't prove anything about glyphosate or GMO-crops.            

You can't prove a negative like absolute lack of negative effects, but there's no real evidence for normal exposure to glyphosate, including normal occupational exposure assuming normal precautions, constitutes a health risk, absolutely none. 

Monsanto was villainized by Greenpeace and other "environmental" organisations well before roundup-ready crops, mostly due to other "GMO"-crops being so great target for made up FUD. Huge amounts of effort has been put into finding or fabricating "evidence" for anything associated with "GMOs" and Monsanto, and especially Monsanto's "GMOs" specifically being dangerous. Potential risks of glyphosate has also been objectively studied in a very large number of studies, including replication of most studies that claimed to shown any level of health risk, showing no consistent health risks. Claiming that only a very small number of studies have studied potential risks with glyphosate is just not true.                                    

While consumption of large amounts of glyphosate probably could affect gut microbes, normal use of a herbicide does NOT drinking the herbicide, and the idea that consuming enough glyphosate to affect gut microbes could cause cancer is totally irrelevant unless you actually consume that much glyphosate, and it's also completely speculative, you can base the same speculation about anything potentially harmful for bacteria, which kind of includes anything. Too much of anything, and also too little of a lot of things can be bad for bacteria.

Author: @jjohansen86
Content: So, one more aspect of this, which is sort of peripheral: In so many of the clips of protests against Monsanto, most of the signs that you see are "No GMOs" and similar. But equating GMOs with Monsanto is incorrect: Monsanto does produce the mostly widely used genetic modification in their Roundup Ready series of crops, but that's not the only thing out there. Golden Rice is also a GMO, it's rice that has been genetically modified to produce beta carotene, a precursor found in foods like carrots that your body can easily use to produce Vitamin A. Golden Rice exists purely for humanitarian reasons, as it can prevent blindness and death as a result of Vitamin A deficiency. However, the strong association that many have between GMOs and Monsanto leads them to oppose GMOs so generally that this negative association has been a drag on the adoption of Golden Rice and research into similar purely humanitarian GMOs. My point is that we do need to acknowledge how these two things are separate: If you recognize the good that GMOs can do, that doesn't mean that you have to believe that they're all good or that Monsanto is good; if you recognize that evil that Monsanto has done, that doesn't mean that you have to condemn all possible uses of this technology. We need to consider the development of technologies like genetic modification on a case by case basis with care.

Author: @ytvancedailey
Content: All things being equal, crop production is higher when herbicides are used. In wealthy countries the impact of not using herbicides would likely be increased food costs for the citizens but would not likely create food scarcity. However, in third world countries lower crop yields and higher costs could lead to increased hunger and malnutrition. In a perfect world farmers could grow just as much food at the same cost without herbicides but that is not the case which is why farmers, quite reasonably, use herbicides. Perhaps herbicides will not be needed in the future but until then a search for safe and effective herbicides should continue. Independent scientific studies are essential to evaluate safety issues. The court system with lawyers with financial conflicts of interest and juries lacking the scientific training to evaluate extremely technical issues are not equipped to evaluate whether a product is acceptably safe. (not that any product is ever as safe as distilled water.) The courts however can and should evaluate corporate fraud and deception. Not being a scientist I can't evaluate the risk of death from Roundup myself and I am not sure I trust people on either side of the issue since many of them have vested interests or they are no more qualified than I am to understand the science. However, food insecurity is a real problem and people are dying because either food is in short supply or is affordable.

Correlation is not causation. Funny how they didn't bring up the hundreds of millions of people that use glyphosate daily and who never got cancer. But it is far easier to cherry-pick the data they want and use your emotions to blame a faceless corporation. 

Fifth, the people that claim Monsanto "wrote the papers" to disprove it provided no evidence to support that. That's called a "conspiracy theory."

Sixth, lawyers are not known for their trustworthiness, especially when it comes to making billions of dollars from a class-action lawsuit. All they have to do is convince non-scientists that it "could". And they convinced the head of the IARC to make the "possible carcinogen" determination to make that easier for them.

Lastly, humans utilize dozens of *ACTUAL* carcinogens daily, and somehow, people demonize Monsanto for something they've never actually been able to prove happens. It's almost like the whole thing was cooked up as an excuse to file the class-action lawsuits to make stupid amounts of money. But it's not like lawyers don't do that all the time, right? Filing hundreds of fake lawsuits to either bankrupt a company for no reason, or to pay a claim to "settle" the fake lawsuits because it would be cheaper than fighting them all. If they weren't fake lawsuits, they would have only needed to prove it in court one time. Weird how that didn't happen. What's better for the company: fight a thousand lawsuits costing 10-20 billion dollars, or "settle" for 1 billion? You're a science channel. Rely on the science, not the people that make the claims who are selling a book about it. There's a reason they went for "possible carcinogen" and not "carcinogen." The lymph vessels transport excess, waste-charged fluid away from the intercellular spaces and return it to the bloodstream. Each body cell is bathed in fluid made of materials derived from blood plasma and other blood elements which diffuse through the capillary walls. The fluid acts as a go-between medium for the transfer of vital materials from the blood to the cells, and for cellular debris away from the intercellular environment into the blood. Since the blood doesn’t come into direct contact with the cells (except in the spleen), one of the main functions of blood is to supply and renew lymph to all body tissues. Thus, the blood feeds the lymph, and the lymph feeds the cells. To appreciate the importance of lymph, one should consider that the body contains 3-times more lymph than blood.

In this modern era, in which food, water and air have become chemical soups, the importance of draining the lymphatic system should not be ignored.

Author: @redpandamurphy
Content:
43:38 not a correction this time but the term for this would probably be stochastic effects. In radiation, there are two observable types of effects, deterministic and stochastic. Deterministic effects are effects that will likely appear at certain radiation dose levels, such as skin irritation, deformity, and other observable symptoms. Stochastic effects are random effects that do not have a determined dose threshold, so things that are randomly caused but unable to be pinpointed exactly other than to radiation exposure. In radiotherapy, they want to maximise the deterministic effects rather than the stochastic effects and they do a bunch of math and science to figure out how to do that (I learned aboit it for college but I haven't been in college for over 3 months so I've forgotten much about it). Stochastic effects can also be evident only after the person has a child, where that child can develop deformities, be at risk for more diseases, or potentially die early. If you're wondering why I would say it's a stochastic effect, it affects the genes and while there is little to no evidence to suggest that products treated with it or that only a small bit of roundup exposure can cause NHL, the farmers were exposed to a lot of it while working in the fields, thereby increasing their chance that they could develop NHL. Deterministic effects would mean that all people who were exposed to it above a certain threshold would develop NHL, but some farmers that were exposed to more may have had less serious NHL and vice versa. Science is fun but also a pain.

Author: @thespacepeacock
Content:
The final minute or so of this video is the most significant. Corporations and politicians being able to influence academia to serve their own needs is exactly why stuff like this happens. When you take something thats meant to be an objective, uncorruptable beacon of science and truth and turn it into a means of mass influencing public perception, rewriting the truth becomes essentially trivial. Academic bias (whether intentional or not) is one of the most destructive weapons we posses in today’s Information Age.

This story itself is rather tragic imo. It’s yet another case of some inventor trying to fix a genuine problem with all the right intentions, being ruined by a company that was allowed to get too greedy. A truly harmless pesticide would be amazing for increasing crop yields and making food more abundant, so less people have to suffer from hunger. GMOs are likewise an amazing technology with enormous potential for improving the way we grow our food, but when they’re used for whats essentially biological warfare all of that potential is washed down the drain and they get a bad rep instead. Monopolies arent inherently bad, but when they’re allowed to mingle with science and politics and employ all kinds of dirty tactics to keep their profits up, we’re doing something wrong. And to think most if not all of this mess could have been avoided if the seed patents had just been free for everyone to use.

Content: When I researched this back in 2010, I also came across reports of farms getting ruined by roundup ready alfalfa. Alfalfa produces both non-hard seed (sprouts immediately) and hard seed (can sit dormant in soil for years). If you try to plant something else in the same field or the alfalfa seeds blow into someone else's field, the alfalfa competes with the crops you're trying to grow and acts like a super weed. Even if you think you've gotten rid of it, those hard seeds can sprout after a year or a couple years, and you have more alfalfa in your field that you can't get rid of with herbicide.

Author: @antoniusweezel876
Content:
This is a pretty badly framed video, and even does the "We're going to get comments from Monsanto shills!" to pre-emptively deflect criticism (Never grown a plant in my life unless you count watering some gourds, never worked for an ag or chemical company in my life, I just graduated with a biological sciences degree and have done some research on this topic)

It completely ignores that it's not just GMO seeds that are routinely patented because IP law applies to novel crops too, it frames "This pesticide + resistant crop is so good it out-competes everything else" as "Sinister company forces monopoly on farmers", "company making thing involved in and funding studies about safety of that thing" (Who else is supposed to research that, exactly? Taxes pay for the testing and companies pocket the profits is basically how it already works with how much research was originally publicly funded, this would be even MORE of that) as "They were obviously manipulating these studies" with some pretty tenuous links based on circumstantial quotes. Basic business PR/customer outreach is framed as "covering things up" and "manipulating narratives". Something else that hasn't been mentioned here is that farmers and agricultural workers have a greatly increased risk of ALL Cancers - because they're routinely exposed to a lot of certain carcinogens (sunlight, heavy vehicle exhaust fumes, mycotoxins in grains, increased exposure to zoonotic pathogens etc etc) so it's easy to associate almost anything a farmer interacts with, with an increased cancer risk. 

Lawsuits also do not establish scientific fact - lawyers and judges are not scientists or trained to interpret scientific evidence or studies - and as much as monsanto had a financial incentive to defend their biggest money maker, lawyers have the same to create and win these lawsuits that are linking a very common type of cancer with a very common herbicide. It's even more important to remember that fact under the current US presidency with people like RFK Jr in positions of power while the president and his lackeys routinely ignores the law, because it's entirely possible we see similar efforts against vaccines soon.

And i'm not saying the practices of companies (and ALL companies operate like this under capitalism) are good. If I had my way research would be state/socially funded, the results would be freely available for all to use and decisions about public health and safety would be fully independent and backed by rigorous scientific investigation. But monsanto and glyphosates are both boogeymen that have been built up by a pretty concerted effort from anti GMO activist groups and the wellness/organic farming industry, to the point that those messages have overshadowed actual critical thought and research

Author: @andreafinocchio1315
Content:
I studied plant biotechnology for the better part of my life and I strongly believe in GMOs' potential to better agriculture. This video, from a channel I keep in very high regard and respect was disheartening. I do not want to defend Monsanto in any way and I dislike about every big corporation and their shady practices but this video glosses over the fact that there the facto no evidence of glyphosate being harmful to humans in any of the large cohort studies performed in the last 20 years and the evidence in the papers that prompted those large cohort studies is shaky at best. 

Glyphosate allows a massive reduction in herbicide usage: where you would previously need a cocktail of different herbicides in large amounts now you can spray less and only one. It's a false choice to just say "let's not use glyphosate": but what is the alternative? Getting back to agent orange? Spraying large amounts of other herbicides? Are we sure they are safe? In modern agriculture reducing chemicals usage inevitably results in yield loss, can we afford it? 

Monsanto not allowing farmers to not keep seeds is a dick move but it's pretty irrelevant today. Large scale farmers mostly buy their seeds every season to make sure they are free of pests and that they all have the same genetic and predictable yield. I would be surprised if the transgene for glyphosate resistance wouldn't be lost by a significant portion of plants after a couple of generations, with obvious problems in terms of crop yield.

I am against big corporations and in favour of public research so I am not a fan of Monsanto but I felt the video did a really bad job in separating the good science (I mean the idea itself is bloody genius)   from the obvious wrongdoings of Monsanto.

Although a drop in the ocean, I hope this comment can repair some of the damage. I still think @veritasium is a wonderful channel and one of the best parts of YouTube.

Author: @Mek1919
Content:
Monsanto did nothing wrong, People love to shout ‘CANCER!’ before they’ve even read a single study. So let me set the record straight, because I actually work here, and I’m tired of watching the same myths circle around like an echo chamber.”

I get it—Monsanto’s name sounds like a villain in a bad sci-fi movie. You hear “chemicals,” you imagine some shadowy lab where we cackle over test tubes. The reality? It’s a group of scientists, toxicologists, and engineers who spend years running tests so products don’t harm people. Believe it or not, most of us actually care about the food we put on our own family’s plates.

Let’s talk about the “carcinogen” label everyone throws around. The World Health Organization’s IARC report didn’t call glyphosate a death sentence—it called it a “probable carcinogen.” Guess what else is in that category? Red meat, hot drinks, and working night shifts. So unless you’re ready to swear off steak, coffee, and your 24/7 TikTok habits, maybe consider the nuance.

Here’s the kicker: dose matters. If you drank a swimming pool’s worth of caffeine, that’d be toxic. Same with salt. Same with water. Glyphosate is applied at levels hundreds of times lower than what toxicology studies ever flag as risky. That’s why regulators in the U.S., Europe, Canada, and Australia—who don’t exactly agree on much—have all said it’s safe when used as directed.

Is it perfect? No chemical is. But without it, farmers would need to rely on older, harsher herbicides, plow fields more (which increases carbon emissions), and jack up food prices. That’s not evil—that’s trade-offs.

So before you picture us as cartoon villains twirling our mustaches, maybe ask why every major regulatory agency hasn’t banned it. Spoiler: because the science doesn’t back the fearmongering.

End of rant. Back to watching this video with my coffee (yep, another “probable carcinogen”).
